old definition: Say this after the customer confirms their details. It tells them you have saved the information and everything is official.
new definition: You say this to tell someone you will save their new information.
old example: Marcus confirmed everything was correct. Riley said: Perfect — I will update that in our system now. You will receive a confirmation email within a few minutes.
new example: Thank you. I will update that in our system.

old definition: A request to buy a specific product or service. When a customer places an order, they confirm they want to buy.
new definition: A request to buy a product or service.
old example: Marcus called Riley and said: I want to place an order for fifteen units of the Standard Plan. Riley said: Perfect — I will process your order now.
new example: I want to place an order for fifteen units.

old definition: The number or amount of something. In sales, quantity means how many units or items the customer wants to buy.
new definition: The number or amount of something.
old example: Riley asked Marcus: What quantity do you need? Marcus said: We need fifteen — one for each person on the team.
new example: What quantity do you need?

old definition: To say yes and make something certain. When you confirm an order, both sides agree on the details.
new definition: To say yes and make something certain.
old example: Riley checked all the details and said: Shall I confirm your order? Marcus said: Yes — fifteen units, delivery on Friday.
new example: Can you confirm my order, please?

old definition: One single item in an order. When companies buy software or products, they often count in units.
new definition: One single item in an order.
old example: Marcus said: We have fifteen people on our team, so we need fifteen units. Riley said: Fifteen units — I will check if they are all available.
new example: We need fifteen units for our team.

old definition: Ready to buy or use right now. If a product is available, the customer can order it today.
new definition: Ready to buy or use right now.
old example: Marcus asked if the plan was ready. Riley said: Let me check — yes, fifteen units are available. We can deliver them by Friday.
new example: Yes, fifteen units are available today.

old definition: The process of sending products to the customer after they order. In B2B sales, delivery can also mean when software access is set up.
new definition: Sending a product to the customer after they order.
old example: Marcus asked: When can you deliver? Riley said: When would you like delivery? We can have everything ready by the end of the week.
new example: Delivery will be on Friday.

old definition: The final amount — the full price after counting all units. We say 'your total comes to' when we give the final price.
new definition: The full price after you count everything.
old example: Riley confirmed the price clearly: Your total comes to $750 for fifteen units. That is $50 per unit per month.
new example: The total is $750 for fifteen units.

old definition: To handle or complete something officially. When you process an order, you start preparing it and send a confirmation.
new definition: To work on something officially, like an order.
old example: Marcus said he was ready. Riley said: I will process that for you now — you will receive a confirmation email in a few minutes.
new example: I will process your order now.

old definition: The key question for taking an order. Use 'many' — not 'much' — because you are counting individual units. Always ask this before confirming any details.
new definition: A question you ask to find out the number of items someone wants.
old example: Marcus said he wanted to buy the Standard Plan. Riley responded: Great — how many would you like? We need to know the quantity before we can process anything.
new example: You want the Standard Plan? How many would you like?

word: LET ME CHECK IF THAT IS AVAILABLE
old definition: A professional way to verify that you have the product in stock before confirming. It shows you are careful and organised — never promise what you have not checked.
new definition: A polite phrase you say before you promise a product is in stock.
old example: Marcus asked for twenty units. Riley said: Let me check if that is available. She looked at the system and said: Yes — twenty units are ready for you.
new example: You need twenty? Let me check if that is available.

old definition: Use this when all the details are agreed. It is a polite, professional way to close the conversation and move to the next step.
new definition: A polite question you ask when all the details are agreed.
old example: Riley had the quantity, the price, and the delivery date. She said: Shall I confirm your order? Marcus said: Yes, go ahead.
new example: We have the price and date. Shall I confirm your order?

old definition: Ask this after you confirm the quantity and availability. It shows you are organised and ready to complete the order.
new definition: A question you ask to find out the day the customer wants the product.
old example: Marcus confirmed fifteen units. Riley then asked: When would you like delivery? Marcus said: We need it by the end of next week.
new example: We have fifteen units ready. When would you like delivery?

old definition: Use this to state the final price. Always say 'your total comes to' — not 'the price is' or 'it costs'. It sounds professional and clear.
new definition: A phrase you use to tell the customer the final price.
old example: Riley confirmed the order details and said: Your total comes to $750 for fifteen units. That is the final price, including everything.
new example: Your total comes to $750.

word: I WILL PROCESS THAT FOR YOU NOW
old definition: Say this to close the order professionally. It tells the customer that the work is starting and they will hear back soon.
new definition: A phrase you say to tell the customer you are starting their order.
old example: Marcus confirmed everything. Riley said: Perfect — I will process that for you now. You will receive a confirmation email within a few minutes.
new example: Thank you. I will process that for you now.

old definition: A person or company that has shown some initial interest in your product but has not yet been qualified as a real opportunity.
new definition: A person or company that has shown early interest in what you sell.
old example: We got 40 new leads from the webinar last week, but most of them still need to be qualified before we pitch.
new example: He checked the new lead, who had visited the website and downloaded resources.

old definition: A qualified potential customer who has the budget, the problem you solve, and the authority to make a buying decision.
new definition: A potential customer who is likely to buy.
old example: Once I confirmed she had the budget and the decision-making authority, she moved from a lead to a genuine prospect.
new example: He met the prospect, who had the budget, the need, and the authority.

old definition: A structured, persuasive presentation of your product that connects its value directly to the prospect's specific situation.
new definition: A short presentation that tries to persuade people to buy something.
old example: A good pitch isn't a generic walkthrough — it references exactly what the prospect told you during the discovery call.
new example: He gave his pitch about the new laptop to the people around the table.

old definition: Contact made after an initial meeting or pitch to keep the relationship alive, answer questions, and move the deal forward.
new definition: Contact you make after a meeting to continue the conversation.
old example: Most deals are won in the follow-up, not the first meeting — consistent contact builds trust over time.
new example: She made a follow-up call after sending the proposal.

old definition: To complete a sale by getting the customer's commitment; the moment a prospect agrees to buy.
new definition: To complete a sale when the customer agrees to buy.
old example: If you have done the groundwork properly, the close should feel like a natural next step, not a high-pressure moment.
new example: She smiled and shook his hand to close the sale.

old definition: The set of all active deals at different stages of the sales process, from first contact to close.
new definition: All the deals a company is working on, at different stages.
old example: Our pipeline looks healthy — we have 12 prospects at pitch stage and three that are close to closing.
new example: Our pipeline has five stages, from prospect to closed.

old definition: To assess whether a lead is a genuine sales opportunity by checking their budget, need, and decision-making authority.
new definition: To check if a lead is suitable to become a customer.
old example: Before you invest time in any relationship, qualify the lead — it saves hours of work on deals that were never going to close.
new example: She used her laptop to qualify the lead by checking budget, need, and authority.

old definition: To build a relationship with a prospect over time through consistent, valuable contact until they are ready to make a decision.
new definition: To help a relationship grow by giving regular care and attention.
old example: Not every prospect is ready to buy immediately — some need nurturing for weeks or months before the timing is right.
new example: He wants to nurture this contact, so he meets her for coffee.

old definition: To progress from one stage of the sales process to the next.
new definition: To go from one stage of a process to the next.
old example: This prospect is moving through the pipeline faster than expected — she went from lead to proposal stage in under two weeks.
new example: The deal is moving through the pipeline and is now at the proposal stage.

old definition: To determine whether a lead meets the criteria to become a real sales opportunity worth pursuing.
new definition: To check if a lead is a good match to become a customer.
old example: Before you book a demo, always qualify the lead — ask about their budget, timeline, and who makes the final decision.
new example: We qualified a lead after checking its budget, need, and authority.

old definition: To reach the final agreement and get the customer's commitment to buy.
new definition: To finish the final agreement with a customer.
old example: We have been nurturing this account for three months — I think we are finally in a position to close the deal this week.
new example: After the proposal and negotiation, they were able to close a deal.

old definition: To contact someone again about a specific conversation, proposal, or question.
new definition: To contact someone again about something discussed earlier.
old example: I sent the proposal on Tuesday — I need to follow up on it before the end of the week or we risk losing momentum.
new example: She is following up on the proposal with a phone call.

old definition: A question used to ask where a particular deal currently sits in the sales process.
new definition: A question that asks which step something has reached in a process.
old example: At what stage is the Harmon deal? I want to make sure we have the right support in place before the next call.
new example: At what stage is the Acme Corp deal for $120,000?

old definition: To deliver a targeted, persuasive presentation of your product to a specific prospect.
new definition: To present a product or idea to someone to persuade them.
old example: I pitched to their entire procurement team last Thursday — they asked a lot of questions, which is always a good sign.
new example: He pitches to the older man, showing a smart solution on the screen.

old definition: The first part of a call where you introduce yourself, build brief rapport, and set the tone before moving to business.
new definition: The first part of a call or talk, when you greet someone and begin.
old example: A strong opening puts the prospect at ease — it signals that you are organised and that their time will be well spent.
new example: He smiles at the camera and gives a friendly opening to the video call.

old definition: The clear, specific reason for the call — stated early so the prospect knows why they are talking to you.
new definition: The reason why you do something or why you call someone.
old example: Stating your purpose in the first 60 seconds removes uncertainty and gives the prospect something concrete to respond to.
new example: He explains the purpose of the call while he types on his laptop.

old definition: A brief outline of what the call will cover, shared at the start to set expectations and demonstrate structure.
new definition: A list of the things that will be discussed in a meeting or call.
old example: I always share a quick agenda at the top of a call — it tells the prospect exactly where we're going and makes the time feel controlled.
new example: He looks at the agenda on his laptop while he talks on the phone.

old definition: A warm, comfortable relationship built through conversation — the feeling that you are talking to someone who genuinely understands you.
new definition: A friendly relationship where people understand each other and feel comfortable.
old example: Good rapport doesn't require small talk for its own sake — it comes from listening carefully and reflecting back what you hear.
new example: The two men smile and talk easily, so they already have good rapport.

old definition: A concern, doubt, or reason a prospect raises for not moving forward — a natural and expected part of every sales call.
new definition: A reason you give for disagreeing with something or not wanting it.
old example: An objection is not a rejection — it is usually a question in disguise that tells you exactly what the prospect needs to hear.
new example: He has an objection about the price and explains his worry to the other man.

old definition: An agreement or promise to take a specific next step — the concrete outcome you are working toward at the end of every call.
new definition: A promise or agreement to do something.
old example: Every call should end with a commitment — even a small one. 'I'll send the document and you'll read it by Friday' is a commitment.
new example: She smiles and points to the next step, hoping for a commitment.

old definition: To move deliberately from one phase of the conversation to the next using a signalling phrase.
new definition: To move from one part of a conversation or activity to the next.
old example: Knowing how to transition between phases keeps the call feeling structured rather than like a sales pitch that wandered off course.
new example: She smiles at the man and begins to transition to the next topic.

old definition: To summarise the key points of a conversation before moving to the next step or ending the call.
new definition: To repeat the main points of something in a short way.
old example: Always recap what you heard before you make your offer — it shows you listened and connects your solution directly to their words.
new example: She smiles at her laptop and recaps the three key points of the meeting.

word: THE REASON FOR MY CALL IS
old definition: State the purpose of the call clearly and early — removes ambiguity and gives the prospect something to engage with.
new definition: A phrase you use at the start of a call to say why you are calling.
old example: The reason for my call is that your colleague Priya mentioned you'd been looking at ways to improve your pipeline visibility.
new example: The reason for my call is to confirm our meeting on Thursday afternoon.

old definition: A phrase used to signal the start of the structured part of the call, often followed by a quick agenda.
new definition: A phrase you use to say something first, before the main discussion starts.
old example: Before we dive in, I just want to give you a quick outline of what I'd like to cover — that way you know exactly where we're going.
new example: Before we dive in, would you like some water or a coffee?

old definition: A soft, professional transition into the discovery phase — signals that you want to understand before you recommend.
new definition: A polite phrase used to begin asking someone a question about a topic.
old example: Can I ask you about your current setup? I want to make sure anything I show you is actually relevant to your team.
new example: Can I ask you about your team and how you work now?

word: BASED ON WHAT YOU'VE TOLD ME
old definition: The key phrase for transitioning into your offer — it signals that your solution is built on what you heard, not on a generic script.
new definition: A phrase meaning you are using the information that someone gave you.
old example: Based on what you've told me — the manual reporting and the team of 15 reps — here's what I think would genuinely help.
new example: Based on what you've told me, this plan should help your company grow.

word: WHAT I'D LIKE TO PROPOSE IS
old definition: A professional way to introduce your offer or recommendation — confident but not pushy.
new definition: A polite phrase used to introduce a suggestion or plan.
old example: What I'd like to propose is a short demo where I show you exactly how the pipeline view and automated reporting would work for a team your size.
new example: What I'd like to propose is a new plan with ongoing support.

old definition: The phrase that signals you are moving toward a concrete commitment — what happens after this call.
new definition: A phrase used to say what will happen or be done after this.
old example: As a next step, would you be open to a 30-minute demo next week? I can have the dashboard set up with your team's structure before we even start.
new example: As a next step, I can schedule a demo and share the proposal.

old definition: Real and sincere — coming from actual interest rather than a script or performance.
new definition: Real and sincere, not pretending.
old example: Customers can tell the difference between a genuine question and a scripted opener — authentic curiosity builds trust far faster.
new example: She showed genuine interest in the man's work during their meeting.

old definition: The ability to understand and share what another person is experiencing or feeling.
new definition: The ability to understand how another person feels.
old example: Showing empathy when a prospect mentions a difficult quarter costs nothing — and it changes the entire tone of the conversation.
new example: I felt empathy for my colleague when she lost her biggest client.

old definition: To respond to someone's warmth or openness with the same energy — to give back what you receive.
new definition: To give back the same kind of action or feeling you received.
old example: When a prospect opens up about their challenges, reciprocate with a relevant experience rather than moving straight to your pitch.
new example: The man shared his plans over lunch, so his guest chose to reciprocate.

old definition: To show clearly that you have heard or noticed something the other person said or experienced.
new definition: To show that you have heard or noticed what someone said.
old example: Before moving on, acknowledge what they just told you — it signals that you were actually listening.
new example: The salesman nodded to acknowledge the customer's worry about the car's price.

old definition: Paying careful, genuine attention to what someone is saying rather than just waiting for your turn to speak.
new definition: Listening or watching carefully and giving full attention.
old example: Being attentive in the first five minutes of a call gives you everything you need to personalise the next fifty.
new example: She stayed attentive on the phone and wrote down every detail.

old definition: Shared between two or more people — a mutual connection, a mutual interest, a mutual experience.
new definition: Shared by two or more people.
old example: Finding a mutual connection or shared experience is one of the fastest ways to move from stranger to trusted contact.
new example: The two men found a mutual interest while looking at the tablet.

old definition: Open and honest in a way that feels refreshing — willing to speak directly and personally.
new definition: Honest and direct when speaking.
old example: Being candid about the purpose of your call — rather than disguising it — is itself a form of rapport-building.
new example: He was candid with the customer about the price at the car showroom.

old definition: Light, casual conversation on non-business topics — used to build comfort and connection before getting to the point.
new definition: Friendly, light conversation about everyday topics.
old example: Small talk is not wasted time — it is the foundation that makes everything else in the conversation easier.
new example: The two men made small talk over coffee at the café.

old definition: Follow up on something the prospect mentioned previously — shows you were listening and remembered.
new definition: A question you ask to find out the result of something.
old example: You mentioned you had a big product launch last week — how did it go? I've been wondering how it landed.
new example: You had an important meeting yesterday. How did it go?

old definition: Reference something specific you found out about the prospect — through research, LinkedIn, or a previous conversation.
new definition: A phrase used to say you saw or found out something.
old example: I noticed that your team has grown quite significantly this year — that must have brought some interesting challenges with it.
new example: I noticed that your company has grown a lot this year.

old definition: Show empathy by acknowledging the prospect's experience without projecting or over-explaining.
new definition: A phrase used to show you understand how someone feels.
old example: A product launch in Q4 — I can imagine the pressure that puts on the whole team.
new example: I can imagine how stressful that week was for you.

old definition: Connect what the prospect says to a relevant experience or example — builds mutual ground without making it about you.
new definition: A phrase used when what you hear makes you think of something similar.
old example: That reminds me of a conversation I had with a similar team last quarter — they described exactly the same challenge.
new example: That reminds me of a project my team finished last year.

word: ITS GOOD TO PUT A FACE TO THE NAME
old definition: A warm phrase for the first time you speak to someone you have only communicated with by email or message.
new definition: A friendly phrase for meeting someone you only knew by name.
old example: Emma — it's great to finally speak. It's good to put a face to the name after all our back-and-forth over email.
new example: It's good to put a face to the name. We have only emailed so far.

old definition: A natural transition phrase that moves the conversation from small talk to the business topic without it feeling abrupt.
new definition: A phrase used to move to a new topic connected to what was said.
old example: Speaking of which — what you just said about scaling the team is actually exactly why I wanted to connect today.
new example: Speaking of which, how is your new project going at work?

old definition: A specific problem or frustration that a customer experiences regularly — the thing that is making their work harder than it should be.
new definition: A problem that regularly causes frustration or difficulty for someone.
old example: Before you pitch anything, you need to understand their pain points — what is actually slowing them down day to day.
new example: Her biggest pain point is the endless emails, paperwork and deadlines.

old definition: A point in a process that slows everything else down — where work gets stuck or piles up.
new definition: A point in a process where work slows down or gets stuck.
old example: The bottleneck in their pipeline was the approval process — deals were getting stuck there for weeks before anyone followed up.
new example: The approval stage is the bottleneck, so every deal waits there for days.

old definition: The thing that matters most right now — what the team or business is focused on above everything else.
new definition: The thing that is most important and needs attention first.
old example: Understanding their priorities tells you which problems they are actually motivated to solve and which ones they can live with.
new example: She points to the first item on the board because it is the top priority.

old definition: A temporary solution someone uses because the proper fix is not in place yet — often a sign that a real problem exists.
new definition: A temporary way to deal with a problem when there is no proper solution.
old example: When a prospect describes a workaround, that is a strong signal — it means the problem is real enough that they built something to manage it.
new example: She uses a manual workaround to connect the sales platform and the finance system.

old definition: To identify the root cause of a problem by asking the right questions — like a doctor figuring out what is wrong before prescribing anything.
new definition: To find out the cause of a problem by looking at it carefully.
old example: A good discovery call is not about selling — it is about diagnosing. You are trying to understand the real problem, not just the surface one.
new example: She asks careful questions on the video call to diagnose the problem.

old definition: To ask follow-up questions that go deeper into what the prospect has said — to get beyond the first answer.
new definition: To ask more questions to learn more about something.
old example: When they say 'communication is an issue', probe — ask what that looks like in practice, who it affects, and how long it has been going on.
new example: The shop assistant decides to probe and asks the customer another question.

old definition: To find out something the prospect has not volunteered — often a hidden problem or need that comes out through careful questioning.
new definition: To discover something that was hidden or not known before.
old example: The best discovery questions uncover problems the prospect did not even realise they wanted to talk about.
new example: He asks careful questions to uncover the real reason behind the complaint.

old definition: The capacity a team has to take on new work, change, or initiative — if they have no bandwidth, even a great solution will not get implemented.
new definition: The time and energy a person or team has available for more work.
old example: Before proposing anything, ask about bandwidth — if the team is already at capacity, timing becomes part of the conversation.
new example: The team has little bandwidth this week because capacity is already at ninety percent.

word: WHAT DOES THAT LOOK LIKE IN PRACTICE
old definition: Ask the prospect to describe a problem concretely — move from a general statement to a real, specific example.
new definition: A question that asks for a real, specific example of something.
old example: You mention that handoffs between teams are a problem — what does that look like in practice? Can you walk me through a recent example?
new example: You said the process is messy, but what does that look like in practice?

old definition: Explore the impact of a challenge on the team, the process, or the business — moves the conversation from problem to consequence.
new definition: A question that asks about the results or effects of a problem.
old example: How is that affecting the rest of the team? Are deals slipping because of it, or is it more of a morale issue at this point?
new example: How is that affecting your team, your deals and the general mood?

word: WHAT HAVE YOU TRIED SO FAR
old definition: Find out what solutions the prospect has already attempted — avoids suggesting something they have already ruled out and shows you are listening.
new definition: A question that asks about solutions someone has already used.
old example: What have you tried so far to solve this? I want to make sure I understand what has worked and what has not before I suggest anything.
new example: What have you tried so far, apart from spreadsheets, email and Slack?

word: IF YOU COULD CHANGE ONE THING
old definition: A focus question that helps the prospect identify their single biggest priority — useful when they have described multiple problems.
new definition: A question that asks what is the one most important thing to improve.
old example: If you could change one thing about how your team manages the pipeline right now, what would it be?
new example: If you could change one thing about your reporting process, what would it be?

old definition: A future-state question that helps the prospect articulate what success means to them — gets them thinking about the outcome, not just the problem.
new definition: A question that asks someone to describe the result they want.
old example: What would good look like for you six months from now? If we solve this properly, what changes for your team?
new example: What would good look like for your team in six months?

old definition: Ask the prospect to describe a process, situation, or problem step by step — gives you a full picture rather than a summary.
new definition: A request for someone to explain a process one step at a time.
old example: Walk me through what happens when a new lead comes in — from the moment it enters the system to the first call. I want to understand the full flow.
new example: Walk me through your process, from the first new lead to the final check.

old definition: A point of resistance or difficulty in a process — something that slows things down or creates unnecessary effort without adding value.
new definition: Something that makes a process slower or harder than it should be.
old example: There is a lot of friction in their approval process — every deal has to go through three sign-offs before anyone can move forward.
new example: There is too much friction here, because every document needs three approvals.

old definition: A visible sign that a deeper problem exists — what the customer notices on the surface rather than the real cause underneath.
new definition: A sign that shows there is a bigger problem.
old example: Slow follow-up times are often a symptom of a deeper issue — usually unclear ownership or no agreed process for who picks up what.
new example: Slow replies and unhappy customers are symptoms of a bigger problem.

old definition: The underlying reason a problem exists — as opposed to the symptoms the customer can see. Solving the root cause fixes the problem; solving the symptom only masks it.
new definition: The main reason why a problem happens.
old example: The root cause was not the CRM — it was that no one had defined what stage a deal needed to reach before handing it over.
new example: The root cause of the delays is that nobody owns the handoff.

old definition: The measurable or felt effect a problem has on the business, the team, or an outcome — what the problem is actually costing.
new definition: The strong effect that something has on a person or situation.
old example: Understanding the impact of a problem is what turns a vague complaint into a business case — it answers the question: why does this matter?
new example: The impact is big, with conversion down 23% and revenue down 31%.

old definition: Happening repeatedly — a problem that keeps coming back rather than being solved once, often because only the symptom has been addressed.
new definition: Happening again and again.
old example: If the same issue is recurring every quarter, that is a sign the root cause has never been properly dealt with.
new example: This is a recurring problem, and it keeps coming back every few weeks.

old definition: The point at which a problem becomes serious enough to act on — when the pain is bad enough that doing nothing is no longer acceptable.
new definition: The point where a situation starts to become serious.
old example: Most customers have a threshold — until a problem crosses it, they will live with it. Your job is to find out how close they are to that line.
new example: The pile of files has reached the threshold, and cost and risk are rising.

old definition: Existing beneath the surface — the real reason something is happening, which may not be immediately obvious from the visible symptoms.
new definition: Being the real cause of something, but not easy to see at first.
old example: The underlying issue was not the software — it was that the team had never agreed on a shared definition of what a qualified lead actually was.
new example: The underlying problem is not the software but the team's unclear criteria.

old definition: To express a problem in numbers or measurable terms — to move from 'this is a problem' to 'this is costing us X per month in lost deals'.
new definition: To measure something and say exactly how much or how many.
old example: When you can help a prospect quantify a problem, it becomes much harder to ignore — and much easier to justify solving.
new example: We can quantify it as $247,000 in lost revenue per month.

old definition: Reflect back what you have heard before naming the problem — shows you were listening and gives the prospect a chance to confirm or correct.
new definition: Words you use to say what you think someone means.
old example: It sounds like the main challenge is not generating leads — it is knowing what to do with them once they are in the system.
new example: It sounds like you get many leads, but the system does not handle them well.

word: WOULD YOU SAY THAT IS A
old definition: Gently categorise a problem as a challenge, issue, or need — and check whether the prospect agrees with how you have framed it.
new definition: A polite question to check if a description fits a situation.
old example: Would you say that is a process issue, or more of a people issue? I want to make sure I am framing this correctly.
new example: Would you say that is a process problem, a people problem, or a need?

word: HOW LONG HAS THIS BEEN GOING ON
old definition: Establish how long the problem has existed — a long-standing problem signals urgency and often reveals that previous attempts to fix it have failed.
new definition: A question asking how long a situation has continued.
old example: How long has this been going on? If it has been there for two years, that tells me something different than if it started last quarter.
new example: How long has this been going on? It looks like more than two years.

word: WHAT IS THE IMPACT OF THAT ON
old definition: Move from identifying the problem to understanding its consequences — helps you and the prospect see what the problem is actually costing.
new definition: A question asking what effect something has on something else.
old example: What is the impact of that on your conversion rate? I want to understand not just the problem but what it is doing to the numbers.
new example: What is the impact of that on your conversion rate, which is now 18%?

word: IS THIS SOMETHING THAT COMES UP REGULARLY
old definition: Find out whether a problem is recurring or a one-off — recurring problems are more urgent and more likely to justify investment in a solution.
new definition: A question asking if something happens often or only once.
old example: Is this something that comes up regularly, or was this more of a one-off? I want to know if we are dealing with a pattern or an exception.
new example: Is this something that comes up regularly, or did it only happen on Wednesday?

old definition: Summarise your understanding of the root cause once you have uncovered it — a clear, direct reframing that shows you have gone beneath the surface.
new definition: Words you use to name the main problem after you understand it.
old example: So the real issue is not the volume of leads — it is that no one owns the process once a lead comes in. Is that a fair way to put it?
new example: So the real issue is what happens to leads after they enter the funnel.

old definition: Something a product has or can do. For example, "sends automatic emails" is a feature.
new definition: A part of a product that does a particular thing.
old example: Real-time pipeline tracking is a feature — it tells you what the product can do, but not why that matters to this specific customer.
new example: This calendar has a sync feature that shows her whole team's schedule.

old definition: The good thing a feature does for the customer — why it matters to them.
new definition: A good result that something gives you.
old example: The benefit of real-time tracking is that Marcus can see where every deal is the moment something stalls, without waiting for a rep to tell him.
new example: The biggest benefit for him is seeing every deal update live on his laptop.

old definition: The result after using a product — what is better or different because of it.
new definition: The final result of an action or process.
old example: The outcome we are aiming for is not just better data — it is two or three more closed deals per month that would otherwise have slipped through.
new example: The outcome on his tablet shows $45K more revenue every month.

old definition: Connected to what the customer said or needs. Only talk about things that matter to them.
new definition: Connected to the subject or to what someone needs.
old example: Everything you present should pass one test: is this relevant to what they told me in discovery? If it is not, leave it out.
new example: She only talks about features that are relevant to her client's goals.

old definition: Clear and easy to measure. Not vague — something you can put a number on.
new definition: Real and clear enough to see or measure.
old example: Vague benefits lose deals — 'saves time' means nothing. Tangible benefits win them — 'reduces manual reporting from three hours a week to twenty minutes'.
new example: The results are tangible, because reporting dropped from three hours to twenty minutes a week.

old definition: To show that your product is different from other options — to explain why yours is a better choice.
new definition: To show how one thing is different from another.
old example: You do not need to criticise competitors to differentiate — just show what changes for the customer when they choose you instead.
new example: She uses her tablet to differentiate her product from the old manual way.

old definition: When something feels true or important to someone. A benefit resonates when the customer thinks "yes, that is my problem."
new definition: To feel true or important to someone.
old example: A benefit resonates when the prospect says 'yes, that is exactly the problem' — not when they politely nod and move on.
new example: The health and battery features resonated with the customer looking at the smartwatch.

old definition: To explain a feature in simple, practical words — to say what it means for the customer.
new definition: To change something into simpler words that people understand.
old example: Your job in a pitch is to translate — take what the engineers built and turn it into something the customer can immediately see the value of.
new example: He can translate "real-time data sync API" into plain words for the visitor.

old definition: Use this to say how a feature is good for the customer. It connects the product to what the customer needs.
new definition: A phrase used to say how something is useful to the listener.
old example: The automated follow-up reminders — this helps you make sure no deal goes cold because a rep forgot to check in.
new example: This helps you follow up on time, so no deal slips through.

old definition: Use this to say the most important good thing first, before you explain how it works.
new definition: A phrase used to introduce the most important good point.
old example: The main benefit is visibility — you will always know exactly where every deal is, without having to ask anyone.
new example: The main benefit is real-time visibility of every deal in your pipeline.

word: WHAT THAT MEANS FOR YOU IS
old definition: Use this to explain a feature in a way that is personal and practical for this customer.
new definition: A phrase used to explain how something affects the listener.
old example: We track every touchpoint automatically — what that means for you is that your pipeline data is always accurate, not just when someone remembers to update it.
new example: What that means for you is that your pipeline is always accurate.

old definition: A short linking phrase that connects a feature to its benefit. It keeps your speech natural.
new definition: A phrase used to add the result of what you just said.
old example: Our system sends automatic alerts when a deal has not moved in five days — which means you can intervene before a prospect goes cold, not after.
new example: The system sends an alert after five days, which means you can act early.

old definition: Use this to give a real, everyday example of what the benefit looks like.
new definition: A phrase used to show how something works in real life.
old example: The dashboard updates in real time — so in practice, you could open it at 9am on Monday and see the exact status of every deal without sending a single message to the team.
new example: So in practice, at 9:00 AM you see every deal live on the tablet.

old definition: Use this to show the difference between your product and another option. It makes the benefit clear.
new definition: A phrase used to show how two things are different.
old example: Compared to building a manual spreadsheet that relies on everyone remembering to update it, this runs automatically in the background — no maintenance required.
new example: Compared to manual spreadsheets, the automatic system needs no upkeep.

old definition: A suggestion that something is the best course of action, based on what you know about the person's situation — not a generic opinion.
new definition: A suggestion about what is the best thing to do.
old example: A strong recommendation is specific to the person you are talking to — it should reference what they told you, not just what you usually say.
new example: At the trade show booth, she shows him her recommendation on the tablet.

old definition: Strongly persuasive and difficult to argue against — a compelling recommendation gives someone a clear reason to act.
new definition: Very convincing and hard to say no to.
old example: The most compelling recommendations connect directly to a pain point the prospect named themselves — they cannot easily dismiss something they already said was a problem.
new example: At the airport café, he shows the man a compelling plan on his tablet.

old definition: Uncertainty or reluctance to commit — a prospect's hesitation is useful information, not an obstacle. It tells you what is still unresolved.
new definition: A short pause or doubt before you decide or act.
old example: If there is hesitation after a recommendation, do not push harder — ask what is behind it. There is usually a specific concern you have not addressed yet.
new example: She looks at the car on the tablet with hesitation before answering.

old definition: Designed or adapted specifically for a particular person's situation — the opposite of a generic or one-size-fits-all proposal.
new definition: Made or changed to fit one person's needs.
old example: A tailored recommendation always begins with what you heard — 'based on what you told me' signals that this is not your standard pitch.
new example: In the apartment, the agent shows the client a tailored list of homes.

old definition: Not fully confident or committed — offering something as a possibility rather than a clear view. Useful when you want to leave room for the prospect to push back.
new definition: Not certain or final, and open to change.
old example: When a prospect is risk-averse, a tentative recommendation using 'could' or 'might' feels safer than a confident 'should' — it gives them control.
new example: At the summit, he gives a tentative opinion about the cloud option.

old definition: To state something with confidence and directness — to make your recommendation clearly without excessive hedging or qualification.
new definition: To say something strongly and with confidence.
old example: The best salespeople know when to assert — when you have done the discovery and know the solution fits, a clear recommendation is more respectful than a vague one.
new example: Over lunch, he asserts that the plan on the tablet is the best choice.

old definition: A proposed course of action or offer put forward for consideration — what you are recommending and why it makes sense.
new definition: A plan or offer that someone puts forward for others to consider.
old example: Before you make a proposition, earn the right to make it — a recommendation lands better when the prospect already trusts that you understand their situation.
new example: In the hotel lobby, he explains his proposition to the man using a tablet.

old definition: To persuade someone that something is true or the right course of action — but in sales, the goal is not to convince through pressure, it is through clarity.
new definition: To make someone believe something or agree to do something.
old example: You do not need to convince someone who already recognises the problem — you just need to make the path to solving it feel clear and low-risk.
new example: She points to the tablet and tries to convince the man at her booth.

word: BASED ON WHAT YOU HAVE TOLD ME
old definition: Ground your recommendation in the prospect's own words — signals that you listened and that what follows is tailored, not generic.
new definition: Using the information you gave me as the reason.
old example: Based on what you have told me about your team size and the visibility gap, I would suggest starting with the pipeline dashboard before anything else.
new example: Based on what you have told me, visibility is the best place to begin.

old definition: A confident but non-pushy way to introduce a recommendation — 'would' makes it feel considered rather than prescriptive.
new definition: A polite way to give your idea about what to do.
old example: I would suggest a phased approach — start with the core pipeline tool in month one, and add the reporting layer once the team has adopted the basics.
new example: I would suggest starting with the core tool and adding reports in phase two.

old definition: A softer, lower-commitment entry point — 'could' gives the prospect options and signals that you are not trying to force a particular path.
new definition: A phrase used to offer an easy first step.
old example: You could start with just the manager dashboard — it gives you the visibility you need without requiring any change from the reps at this stage.
new example: You could start with the manager view and add team features later.

old definition: A direct and confident framing — signals that you have a clear, considered view and are willing to state it.
new definition: A phrase used to say what you think is the best choice.
old example: What I would recommend is the full pipeline plan — based on what you described, the core tool alone would not solve the follow-up piece, and you would end up coming back for the rest.
new example: What I would recommend is the plan with all four features selected.

old definition: Show the direct consequence or benefit of following the recommendation — connects your suggestion to a specific outcome the prospect wants.
new definition: A phrase used to say what result or benefit someone will get.
old example: Starting with the dashboard would give you the visibility you mentioned straight away — you would not need to wait for a full rollout to see the impact.
new example: That would give you a live view of your sales on one dashboard.

word: IF I WERE IN YOUR POSITION
old definition: Build empathy and credibility by thinking from the prospect's perspective — signals that your recommendation is personal and honest, not just a sales script.
new definition: A phrase for giving your opinion by imagining you are the other person.
old example: If I were in your position — a growing team, a broken manual process, and deals slipping through — I would want to fix the visibility problem first before adding anything else.
new example: If I were in your position, I would fix the manual process first.

old definition: A reason a prospect gives for not moving forward — a concern, doubt, or barrier that needs to be addressed before they can commit.
new definition: A reason someone gives for not agreeing or not wanting to go ahead.
old example: An objection is not a rejection — it is a signal that the prospect is still engaged but needs something resolved before they feel ready to move.
new example: He raises an objection about the price and the timing.

old definition: A worry or doubt that is preventing someone from making a decision — something that feels unresolved or risky to them.
new definition: A worry about something important that makes a decision difficult.
old example: The most common concerns in B2B sales are price, timing, and risk — but the real concern is often something different beneath the surface.
new example: His biggest concern is the risk, so he is thinking carefully.

old definition: To acknowledge that a concern or objection is legitimate and understandable — not to agree with it, but to show you take it seriously.
new definition: To show that someone's worry or feeling is reasonable and understandable.
old example: Validating an objection does not mean you are conceding the point — it means the prospect feels heard, which makes them far more open to your response.
new example: The jar of stones helps validate the worry about high cost.

old definition: To present an objection or situation from a different angle — showing it in a new light that reduces its impact or makes it easier to work with.
new definition: To describe something in a different way so it looks less negative.
old example: When a prospect says 'it is too expensive', reframe the conversation around the cost of not solving the problem — not just the cost of the solution.
new example: She tries to reframe the upfront cost as long-term value.

old definition: To show genuine understanding of how the prospect feels — not just what they are saying, but why it matters to them.
new definition: To understand and share how another person feels.
old example: Empathising with a concern is not the same as agreeing with it — it signals that you understand their world well enough to take their hesitation seriously.
new example: She listens and tries to empathise with the woman's worries about the home.

old definition: A delaying tactic — when a prospect gives a vague reason for not deciding, without saying no directly. Usually a sign that something else is unresolved.
new definition: To delay a decision or action, usually by avoiding a clear answer.
old example: 'We will think about it' is often a stall rather than a genuine objection — the real issue is usually that the value is not yet clear or the risk feels too high.
new example: The customer stalls by raising his hand and avoiding a clear answer.

old definition: To successfully address an objection so that it is no longer a barrier — not by arguing, but by providing what the prospect needs to feel confident.
new definition: To deal with a problem successfully so it is no longer a difficulty.
old example: You do not overcome an objection by talking louder or pushing harder — you overcome it by understanding what is really behind it and addressing that specific thing.
new example: She shows him the watch to help overcome his doubts.

old definition: To deal with a concern directly and specifically — to give it the attention it deserves rather than deflecting or moving past it.
new definition: To deal with a problem or question carefully and directly.
old example: When a prospect raises a concern, address it before moving on — skipping over it signals that you did not listen, or that you have no good answer.
new example: He points at the tablet to address the customer's question about the rings.

old definition: The core acknowledgment phrase — opens your response by showing the prospect that their worry has been heard and taken seriously, before you say anything else.
new definition: A polite phrase that shows you have heard someone's worry and take it seriously.
old example: I understand your concern about the timeline — that is a completely reasonable thing to raise at this stage. Can I share how other teams in a similar position have handled the rollout?
new example: I understand your concern about the delivery time.

word: CAN I ASK WHAT IS BEHIND THAT
old definition: Probe the objection before responding — find out what is really driving the concern so you can address the actual issue, not just the surface statement.
new definition: A polite question asking for the real reason behind what someone said.
old example: When you say the timing is not right — can I ask what is behind that? I want to make sure I understand whether it is a capacity issue, a budget cycle, or something else.
new example: Can I ask what is behind that, the timing or the budget?

old definition: Validate the objection without fully conceding — acknowledges the legitimacy of what the prospect has said while keeping the door open for your response.
new definition: A phrase that shows you accept that someone's point is reasonable.
old example: That is a fair point — the price is higher than some alternatives. What I would say is that the comparison only makes sense if the alternatives actually solve the same problem.
new example: That is a fair point about the cost, and we can also check the fit.

word: WHAT I HEAR YOU SAYING IS
old definition: Reflect back the objection in your own words — confirms you have understood it correctly and gives the prospect a chance to clarify before you respond.
new definition: A phrase used to repeat what someone said, to check you understood.
old example: What I hear you saying is that the value is clear but the timing feels wrong given everything else the team has on right now. Is that a fair summary?
new example: What I hear you saying is that timing and team load are your main worries.

old definition: Signal that you are going to tackle the concern head-on — builds confidence that you are not going to deflect or dodge the difficult question.
new definition: A phrase used to say you will answer a difficult point honestly and clearly.
old example: Let me address that directly — yes, there is an implementation period, and yes, it requires some time from the team. Here is what that actually looks like in practice.
new example: Let me address that directly, the risk, the schedule and the team.

old definition: Turn a stall or soft no into actionable information — asks the prospect to define what would need to be true for them to move forward.
new definition: A question asking what must happen before someone says yes.
old example: I hear you — what would it take for this to feel like the right move? I want to understand what is still unresolved so I can either address it or tell you honestly if I cannot.
new example: What would it take for you to move in next month?

old definition: Money spent with the expectation of a measurable return — the opposite framing of 'cost', which implies spending with nothing coming back.
new definition: Money you put into something hoping to get more money back later.
old example: When you frame the conversation as an investment rather than a cost, the question changes from 'can we afford this?' to 'what do we get back?'
new example: The $25,000 investment is projected to grow by 38.5% in twelve months.

old definition: The measurable benefit or gain you get from an investment — what the product gives back in time, money, deals, or efficiency.
new definition: The profit or benefit you get back from money you spent.
old example: Before you talk about price, be clear on the return — if the return is bigger than the cost, the price conversation becomes much easier.
new example: The projected return on the $25,000 is 175% after twelve months.

old definition: To provide clear evidence or reasoning that something is worth its cost — to make the case that the value outweighs the price.
new definition: To show that something is worth the money or effort it takes.
old example: A strong value conversation does the work of justifying the investment before the prospect even asks about price.
new example: He tries to justify the cost of the robots by showing the five-year savings.

old definition: Able to be expressed in numbers or tracked over time — a measurable benefit is far more persuasive than a vague one.
new definition: Able to be counted or tracked with numbers.
old example: The most compelling value statements are measurable — 'this reduces your reporting time by three hours a week' is harder to dismiss than 'this saves time'.
new example: He points to the measurable results on the screen, like the 47% drop in downtime.

old definition: Real but difficult to quantify — benefits like team confidence, morale, or reduced stress that do not always show up directly in a spreadsheet.
new definition: Real, but hard to measure or touch.
old example: Do not ignore intangible value — a team that is less stressed and more confident performs better, even if you cannot put a clean number on it.
new example: The team smiles around the table, and their good morale is an intangible benefit.

old definition: Getting more output with the same or less input — doing things faster, with fewer resources, or with less effort.
new definition: Doing work well without wasting time, money, or effort.
old example: Improving efficiency is one of the easiest value cases to make — if you can show how many hours per week a team gets back, the maths usually does the work for you.
new example: He explains that the cleaning robot brings a 52% improvement in efficiency.

old definition: The balance between what you give up and what you gain — every purchase involves a trade-off, and making that trade-off explicit is part of the value conversation.
new definition: Giving up one thing in order to get something else you want.
old example: Be honest about the trade-off — the product costs X per month, but based on the deals you described, it recovers that in the first week. That is a trade-off worth making.
new example: The $299 monthly cost is a small trade-off for 23 deals won.

old definition: The difference between cost and return — either the profit a business makes, or the space a product creates between what it costs and what it generates.
new definition: The difference between what something costs and what it earns.
old example: If your product helps a prospect close two more deals a month, calculate what that does to their margin — the value conversation becomes concrete immediately.
new example: With a cost of $2,000 and a return of $8,000, the profit margin is large.

old definition: Directly state the value — 'it is worth X' positions the product in terms of value received, not price paid.
new definition: Used to say that something has enough value to justify its price or effort.
old example: It is worth thinking about this as a monthly investment of X against a return of two to three recovered deals — at your deal size, that calculation is very clear.
new example: It is worth paying a little more for a laptop that lasts five years.

old definition: Quantify the saving in time, money, or effort — make the value tangible by attaching a specific number.
new definition: Used to say how much time or money someone might not have to spend.
old example: This could save you three hours of manual reporting every week — across a team of five, that is fifteen hours you get back to focus on selling.
new example: This could save you about two hours every day on paperwork.

old definition: Show how value grows or compounds over time — helps the prospect see beyond the immediate cost to the longer-term return.
new definition: Used to say that something will become bigger or greater as time passes.
old example: Over time this would increase your conversion rate as the team builds consistent habits — the value compounds as the behaviour embeds.
new example: Over time this would increase our sales in the new region.

word: THINK ABOUT WHAT YOU WOULD SAVE
old definition: Invite the prospect to do their own mental calculation — getting them to work out the value themselves is more persuasive than telling them.
new definition: Used to ask someone to imagine the money or time they would not spend.
old example: Think about what you would save if even one of those three deals a month did not slip through. At your average deal size, that is the whole year paid for.
new example: Think about what you would save on fuel if you worked from home.

old definition: Make the ROI case explicitly — state clearly what the prospect gets back relative to what they spend.
new definition: Used to say what profit or benefit something gives back.
old example: The return on this is not just financial — yes, you recover deals, but you also get back the management time you currently spend chasing updates from the team.
new example: The return on this is about ten percent every year.

old definition: Reframe price by comparing it to the cost of the problem — shifts the reference point from what the solution costs to what the problem costs.
new definition: Used to show how one price looks when you put it next to another.
old example: Compared to the cost of losing three deals a quarter at your deal size, the monthly fee is a small fraction — and that is before you factor in the time your team spends on workarounds.
new example: Compared to the cost of a new car, the repair is very cheap.

old definition: A short, persuasive presentation of a product or idea designed to convince someone to buy, invest, or take the next step. A good pitch is structured, concise, and focused on the listener.
new definition: A short talk that tries to convince someone to buy something or accept an idea.
old example: David walked the client through his pitch, explaining how the product turns their biggest frustration into a win.
new example: He gave the woman a short pitch about the new speaker in the store.

old definition: A specific problem or frustration a customer experiences regularly. The best pitches start here — when the customer hears their own problem described back to them, they stop thinking and start listening.
new definition: A particular problem that regularly annoys or upsets a customer.
old example: The team spotted the pain point immediately — orders were getting stuck between purchase and delivery.
new example: The man pointed out the pain point, and the woman frowned at her tablet.

old definition: A statement that offers something for consideration. A value proposition explains precisely why your product is worth buying — what it delivers, for whom, and why it is better than the alternative.
new definition: An offer or plan that someone presents for other people to consider.
old example: His value proposition was clear: connect your guests, your bookings, and your operations — and watch costs fall.
new example: He explained his proposition to the woman in the hotel lobby over coffee.

old definition: Persuasive, convincing, and hard to ignore. A compelling pitch makes the customer feel that saying no would mean missing out on something genuinely valuable.
new definition: Very convincing and interesting, so that people pay close attention.
old example: Her case was compelling — the data showed a clear trend that everyone in the room could see.
new example: Her talk was compelling, and the audience watched the growth chart closely.

old definition: Brief and clear, with no unnecessary words or information. A concise pitch respects the customer's time — it says everything that matters and nothing that does not.
new definition: Using few words to give the important information clearly.
old example: He kept his message concise — two minutes, three key points, no extra paperwork.
new example: He kept his explanation concise because the woman had a flight soon.

old definition: To have a strong, lasting effect on someone — to feel deeply relevant and true to their situation. When a pitch resonates, the customer feels understood, not sold to.
new definition: To feel true and important to someone because it matches their own experience.
old example: Her pitch really resonated — he could see exactly how the solution would fix his stores.
new example: Her ideas resonated with the café owner because they matched the problems in his shops.

old definition: To express an idea clearly and effectively so the other person can understand it immediately. If you cannot articulate the benefit in one sentence, the customer will not understand it either.
new definition: To explain something clearly in words so that others understand it.
old example: She was able to articulate a complex process as three simple steps.
new example: She could articulate the messy process in three clear steps for the man beside her.

old definition: A potential customer who has not yet bought from you. Every prospect has a problem you can solve — your pitch is the tool you use to make that connection clear.
new definition: A person who might become a customer in the future.
old example: She spotted a strong prospect across the room and moved in to start a conversation.
new example: She noticed a promising prospect reading about the car on his tablet.

word: I KNOW THAT MANY TEAMS LIKE YOURS STRUGGLE WITH...
old definition: The ideal opening line for a pitch — it names the pain point before you mention your product. When a customer hears their own problem, they immediately pay attention.
new definition: A phrase used to say that other similar groups have the same problem.
old example: I know that many teams like yours struggle with too many emails, missed deadlines, and no clear process.
new example: I know that many teams like yours struggle with too many emails and tight deadlines.

word: THAT IS EXACTLY WHAT [PRODUCT] IS DESIGNED TO SOLVE
old definition: The bridge between the problem and the solution. It tells the customer that your product is not a generic tool — it was built specifically for the problem they just confirmed they have.
new definition: A phrase meaning a product was made to fix this exact problem.
old example: That is exactly what this platform is designed to solve — every step of the customer journey, handled.
new example: That is exactly what this system is designed to solve, from the cart to delivery.

old definition: The phrase that introduces the benefit — the measurable outcome the customer will experience. Always follow it with a specific number, time frame, or concrete change.
new definition: A phrase that introduces what happens because of something.
old example: The result is faster service and happier customers — as you can see from the numbers.
new example: The result is shorter waiting times and happier guests in the restaurant.

old definition: A benefit phrase with built-in urgency. The time frame makes the outcome feel real and achievable — it moves the benefit from abstract to concrete.
new definition: A phrase that says something can happen in a short amount of time.
old example: In just three steps, you could be signing the keys to your new apartment.
new example: In just three weeks, you could be holding the keys to this apartment.

old definition: A soft, non-pressuring close. It invites the customer to agree to a next step by framing it as a logical decision — not a commitment. Customers who say yes feel in control.
new definition: A polite way to ask if someone agrees with a suggested plan.
old example: Would it make sense to schedule a quick follow-up before you fly out?
new example: Would it make sense to book a short meeting for next week?

word: WHAT TENDS TO HAPPEN WITHOUT [SOLUTION] IS...
old definition: A phrase for reinforcing the pain point before the solution. It paints a picture of the cost of inaction — which is often more persuasive than describing the product itself.
new definition: A phrase used to describe the usual bad results when something is missing.
old example: Without a solution, teams like yours are left with stockouts, frustrated shoppers, and no early warning.
new example: What tends to happen without a new system is long queues and empty shelves.

old definition: To contact someone again after a previous conversation in order to check progress, provide additional information, or move a decision forward. Always follow up — it signals professionalism and genuine interest.
new definition: To contact someone again after an earlier conversation to check progress or get an answer.
old example: Riley did not wait for Marcus to call her. She followed up two days after the demo: Good morning, Marcus — I'm following up on our call from Tuesday. I wanted to check in on a couple of things.
new example: She follows up with a client by phone after sending the proposal.

old definition: To make brief contact with someone to check where things stand or share a quick update. It is less formal than 'follow up' and is often used for a short check-in rather than a full conversation.
new definition: To contact someone briefly to share news or see how things are going.
old example: Riley said: I'll touch base with you on Friday afternoon to see if you have an answer from the budget review. If anything comes up before then, please don't hesitate to call me.
new example: I'll touch base with you on Friday to hear about the budget review.

old definition: To summarise the main points of a previous conversation. Recapping confirms shared understanding and reminds the customer of what was agreed — without making them re-read a long email.
new definition: To repeat the main points of an earlier conversation in a short summary.
old example: Riley said: I wanted to quickly recap the key points from Tuesday — $35 per user, 10% off for the first three months, and a two-week implementation. Does everything still look right to you?
new example: She smiled and recapped the key points for the client on the video call.

old definition: Not yet done or resolved — still waiting for an answer or action. 'Outstanding questions' are questions that have not been answered yet. Always offer to address outstanding items in your follow-up.
new definition: Not yet finished, paid, or answered.
old example: Marcus said: The team is positive overall, but there are still a couple of outstanding questions. Riley said: I'm glad to hear the response was positive — what are the outstanding questions? I'd like to address them directly.
new example: We still have a few outstanding questions about the contract.

old definition: The energy or force that keeps something moving forward. In sales, momentum is built through consistent follow-up — if you stop, the deal often stalls or dies.
new definition: The force that keeps something moving forward or making progress.
old example: Riley knew that following up quickly was critical: The longer you leave a deal without contact, the harder it is to rebuild momentum. She called Marcus within 48 hours of the demo.
new example: The project lost momentum when two team members left the company.

old definition: A promise or obligation made in a previous conversation. Referencing past commitments in your follow-up reminds both parties of what was agreed and keeps the conversation moving in the right direction.
new definition: A promise to do something, or a duty that you have agreed to.
old example: Riley reminded Marcus of what had been agreed: As a follow-up to our call, I wanted to confirm the commitment we both made — you would share the proposal internally, and I would send the security documentation today.
new example: She pointed at the screen to confirm the commitment both sides made last week.

old definition: Waiting to be dealt with or decided. A pending decision is one that has not been made yet. In a follow-up, you want to understand what is pending and what you can do to help resolve it.
new definition: Waiting to be decided or finished.
old example: Riley asked: Is there anything still pending on your side that I can help with — a question for your IT team, a document for your finance department? I want to make sure nothing is blocking the decision.
new example: The decision is still pending until the finance team replies.

old definition: The ability to take action proactively — without waiting to be asked. Taking the initiative to follow up signals that you are organised, reliable, and serious about the customer's success.
new definition: The ability to act on your own without being told what to do.
old example: Marcus appreciated that Riley had taken the initiative: She didn't wait for me to call — she followed up with answers before I even had time to think of the questions. That kind of service builds trust.
new example: She showed great initiative by fixing the problem before anyone asked.

old definition: The standard opening for any professional follow-up call or email. 'On' links the follow-up to the specific conversation, proposal, or topic being revisited. Never say 'following up about' or 'following up in'.
new definition: A phrase used to say you are contacting someone again about an earlier topic.
old example: Riley called Marcus two days after the demo and said: Good morning, Marcus. I'm following up on our demo call from Tuesday — I wanted to check in on a couple of things and see if your team had any questions.
new example: Hello, I'm following up on our call from Tuesday about the new contract.

old definition: A phrase that connects your current message to a previous conversation. It reminds the customer of shared context without making them re-read notes — and signals that you were paying attention.
new definition: A phrase that refers to something you both talked about earlier.
old example: Riley said: As we discussed on Tuesday, you were particularly interested in the custom reporting feature and the integration with Salesforce. I wanted to address those points directly before your team meeting on Thursday.
new example: As we discussed, the report will be ready by Thursday morning.

word: I WANTED TO CHECK IN ON...
old definition: A gentle, non-pressuring phrase for following up on a specific item — a decision, a question, or an action. It shows you are tracking progress without making the customer feel chased.
new definition: A polite phrase used to ask about the progress of something.
old example: Riley said: I wanted to check in on whether you had a chance to share the demo summary with your team. I know you mentioned Thursday's budget review — I want to make sure you have everything you need beforehand.
new example: I wanted to check in on the report you were preparing for the meeting.

word: COULD YOU LET ME KNOW WHERE THINGS STAND WITH...?
old definition: A professional way to ask for a status update on a pending decision or action. It is direct without being pushy — and gives the customer a clear question to answer.
new definition: A polite question asking about the current situation of something.
old example: Riley said: Could you let me know where things stand with the internal approval? I want to make sure I can support you through that process — whether that means sending additional documentation or arranging another call.
new example: Could you let me know where things stand with the new budget?

old definition: A phrase that links a specific action to the previous conversation. Use it to show that you followed through on something you promised — it demonstrates reliability.
new definition: A phrase used to say what you did after a phone conversation.
old example: Riley wrote in her follow-up email: Following our call on Tuesday, I have attached the security documentation you requested and a side-by-side comparison of our integration options. Please let me know if you need anything else.
new example: Following our call, I sent you the documents you asked for.

word: PLEASE DON'T HESITATE TO REACH OUT IF...
old definition: A professional closing phrase that keeps the door open for the customer to contact you. It signals availability and removes any friction around asking for help.
new definition: A polite phrase meaning you are welcome to contact me if you need anything.
old example: Riley ended the call warmly: Please don't hesitate to reach out if any further questions come up before Thursday — whether it's from you or from the team. I'm here and happy to help with anything.
new example: Please don't hesitate to reach out if you have any questions about the schedule.

old definition: The title of an email that appears before the email is opened. The subject line is the most important part of any sales email — it determines whether the reader opens it or deletes it without reading.
new definition: The short title of an email that you see before you open it.
old example: A strong subject line creates curiosity and gives the reader a reason to open the email — without it, even the best message goes unread.
new example: He read the subject line of each email on his laptop at the event.

old definition: The opening line of an email — 'Hi James,' or 'Dear Mr Chen,' — that sets the tone and level of formality. The greeting should match your relationship with the reader.
new definition: The first words of an email, such as 'Hi James,' or 'Dear Mr Chen,'.
old example: The greeting sets the tone — use the reader's first name to make the email feel personal from the very first line.
new example: She typed a friendly greeting at the top of her email.

old definition: A clear, specific instruction at the end of an email that tells the reader exactly what to do next. A weak call to action is vague. A strong one is direct, easy to act on, and removes any guesswork.
new definition: A sentence that tells the reader what to do next.
old example: A clear call to action tells the reader exactly what to do next — book a call, confirm a date, or simply reply with a yes.
new example: His email ended with a clear call to action asking the customer to book a visit.

old definition: To tailor a message to a specific person or company — using their name, referencing your last conversation, or connecting to something relevant to their business. Personalised emails perform significantly better than generic ones.
new definition: To change a message so it fits one particular person or company.
old example: Personalise the email with details from your last conversation — generic messages get deleted before they are even read.
new example: She will personalise the email with the customer's car and service details.

old definition: The percentage of recipients who actually open an email. Open rate is determined almost entirely by the subject line — a strong subject line can double or triple the number of people who read your message.
new definition: The percentage of people who open an email they receive.
old example: Changing one subject line pushed the open rate from 18% to 68% — every word in the subject line matters.
new example: He checked the open rate for his email campaign on the laptop.
