old definition: The closing phrase of an email before your name — 'Best regards', 'Kind regards', or 'Looking forward to hearing from you'. A good sign-off matches the tone of the email and implies a response is expected.
new definition: The polite words and name at the end of an email.
old example: A professional sign-off includes your name, role, and contact details — everything the reader needs to respond without searching.
new example: She typed her name and phone number in the sign-off.

old definition: Directly connected to the reader's situation, needs, or previous conversation. A relevant email feels personal and considered. An irrelevant email feels like spam — even if the product is excellent.
new definition: Connected to what a person needs or is interested in.
old example: An email is only relevant if it connects directly to what the reader actually needs — everything else feels like spam.
new example: He only kept the ideas that were relevant to the customer's needs.

old definition: Brief and clear, with no unnecessary words or paragraphs. Sales emails should be concise — three short paragraphs is usually enough. If your email requires scrolling, most readers will not finish it.
new definition: Short and clear, using only the words that are needed.
old example: Keep the email concise — three short paragraphs is enough. If it requires scrolling, most readers will not finish it.
new example: She rewrote the long email to make it concise, with three short points.

old definition: One of the most effective subject line patterns in sales email. It creates curiosity, feels personal, and implies the email will be short and easy to read. Always make the topic specific to the reader.
new definition: A common email subject line that introduces a small question on a certain topic.
old example: 'Quick question about your onboarding process' — this subject line feels personal, takes seconds to read, and gets replies.
new example: She wrote 'Quick question about your order' as the email subject.

old definition: A direct, transparent way to open the body of a sales email. It tells the reader immediately why you are writing — no build-up, no small talk. Transparency builds trust and saves the reader's time.
new definition: A phrase you use to explain the reason you are writing.
old example: I'm reaching out because we spoke last week about your reporting workflow and I have something that directly addresses what you described.
new example: He typed, "I'm reaching out because your team had a problem with delivery."

old definition: A connecting phrase that links the email to a previous conversation. It reminds the reader of shared context and signals that this is a personal message — not a template sent to hundreds of people.
new definition: A phrase used to refer back to an earlier conversation.
old example: As we discussed on the call, I am sending over the information you asked for along with a suggested next step.
new example: She wrote, "As we discussed, I will send the contract tomorrow."

old definition: A soft, professional call to action that invites the reader to agree without feeling pressured. It frames the next step as the reader's choice — which makes them more likely to say yes.
new definition: A polite way to ask if someone would like to try or do something.
old example: Would you be open to a 20-minute call this week to walk through how this could work for your team?
new example: She typed, "Would you be open to a short meeting next week?"

word: I'D LOVE TO [ACTION] — WOULD [DAY] AT [TIME] WORK FOR YOU?
old definition: A specific, action-oriented call to action that proposes a concrete next step. By naming a day and time, you make it easy for the reader to say yes or suggest an alternative — rather than leaving everything open-ended.
new definition: A polite way to suggest doing something at a specific day and time.
old example: I'd love to show you the platform — would Thursday at 2pm work for you, or is Friday morning better?
new example: He typed, "I'd love to show you the demo. Would Tuesday at 3pm work for you?"

word: LOOKING FORWARD TO HEARING FROM YOU
old definition: A professional sign-off that implies a response is expected without being aggressive or demanding. Warmer than 'Best regards' alone — and subtly more effective at generating replies.
new definition: A polite way to end a message when you expect a reply.
old example: Looking forward to hearing from you — let me know if Thursday works or if another time suits you better.
new example: She ended the email with "Looking forward to hearing from you."

old definition: The times when someone is free and able to meet or speak. In sales, you always check availability before proposing a specific time — it signals respect for the customer's schedule.
new definition: The times when a person is free to meet or talk.
old example: Always check availability before proposing a time — it shows you respect the other person's schedule and makes it easier to find something that works for both sides.
new example: She shows him her availability, and three free times are highlighted on the calendar.

old definition: A specific period of time reserved for a particular purpose — a meeting slot, a calendar slot, a time slot. Using 'slot' sounds more professional than saying 'time' or 'space'.
new definition: A period of time set aside for a meeting or task.
old example: There is one slot left on Tuesday afternoon — let me know if that works for you and your team.
new example: He points to the one free slot on the tablet calendar.

old definition: Not yet confirmed — provisionally agreed but still subject to change. A tentative meeting has been discussed but not officially confirmed by both sides.
new definition: Agreed for now, but not final and still able to change.
old example: The meeting is tentative for now — I still need to check with a colleague before I can confirm the time.
new example: The meeting is still tentative, so she marks it with a question mark.

old definition: To arrange a meeting for a different time — when the original time no longer works. Handle rescheduling gracefully — it happens often in B2B sales and is not a sign that the customer is disinterested.
new definition: To change a meeting to a different time or day.
old example: Something came up on Monday, so the viewing had to be rescheduled — Wednesday at the same time still works if that suits you.
new example: He moves the viewing to a new time, and the woman smiles.

old definition: A list of topics or items to be covered in a meeting. Sharing the agenda in advance shows professionalism and helps the customer know what to prepare.
new definition: A list of the topics to be covered in a meeting.
old example: A clear agenda was shared before the demo — platform overview, integration options, and onboarding path, so everyone knew exactly what to prepare.
new example: They go through the agenda on the tablet and check off each item.

old definition: To officially agree and finalise a meeting — making it certain rather than tentative. Always confirm a meeting by email so both sides have a written record of the time, date, and format.
new definition: To make something official and certain.
old example: Once both sides agreed on the time, the appointment was confirmed and a calendar invite followed within minutes.
new example: She confirms the appointment, and a green check mark shows it is booked.

old definition: How long a meeting will last. Always state the duration when scheduling — it helps the customer plan their day and signals that you will respect their time.
new definition: The length of time that something lasts.
old example: Always state the duration upfront — thirty minutes for the demo and fifteen for questions, so the client can plan their day around it.
new example: He explains the duration of the presentation using a clock on the screen.

old definition: A digital meeting request sent through a calendar application — such as Google Calendar or Outlook. Sending a calendar invite confirms the meeting officially and puts it in the customer's diary automatically.
new definition: A message that adds a meeting to someone's online calendar.
old example: A calendar invite was sent to everyone on the team — the meeting landed in their diaries automatically and nobody had to chase for confirmation.
new example: She sends the calendar invite to three colleagues from her laptop.

word: WHAT DOES YOUR AVAILABILITY LOOK LIKE...?
old definition: The professional way to ask when someone is free. More polished than 'When are you free?' — it implies you are flexible and puts the customer's schedule first.
new definition: A polite way to ask when someone is free.
old example: What does your availability look like next week? I want to find a time that works around you — I have flexibility on my side.
new example: What does your availability look like next week? I'd like to meet for lunch.

old definition: The standard phrase for proposing a specific meeting time. Always propose two or three options — never just one — so the customer can choose without feeling boxed in.
new definition: A polite way to suggest a specific day and time for a meeting.
old example: Would Thursday at 2pm work for you, or is Friday morning better?
new example: Would Thursday at 3pm work for you?

old definition: A natural, professional phrase for pausing to verify your availability before confirming a time. It signals that you are organised and that your time is also valuable.
new definition: A phrase you say when you want to look at your schedule.
old example: Let me check my calendar — yes, Thursday at 2pm works perfectly. I will hold that slot now and send a confirmation shortly.
new example: Let me check my calendar. I think I'm free on Friday morning.

word: I'LL PUT THAT IN THE DIARY
old definition: To officially note a meeting in your schedule. 'Diary' is the British English term for a personal planner or calendar. This phrase confirms the meeting is now reserved on your side.
new definition: A phrase meaning you will write the plan in your schedule.
old example: I'll put that in the diary right now — you will receive a calendar invite within the next few minutes to confirm the time.
new example: I'll put that in the diary. Your fitting is booked for Monday at ten.

old definition: A polite way to suggest moving a meeting to a later time or different day. 'Push' implies a slight delay rather than a full cancellation — it sounds flexible rather than unreliable.
new definition: A polite way to ask to move something to a later time.
old example: A conflict has come up — could we push that to 3pm instead? Or if Thursday no longer works, I am also free on Friday afternoon.
new example: Could we push that to Thursday? Something came up at lunchtime.

word: I'LL SEND A CALENDAR INVITE TO CONFIRM
old definition: The standard closing phrase after agreeing a meeting time. It tells the customer exactly what to expect next and creates a formal record of the agreed time.
new definition: A phrase meaning you will send an online meeting request to make it official.
old example: I'll send a calendar invite to confirm — it will go to you and your colleague within the next few minutes, along with a brief agenda.
new example: I'll send a calendar invite to confirm. It should reach your phone now.

old definition: The opening section of a presentation where you welcome the audience, establish context, and explain what you will cover. A strong introduction sets expectations and earns attention.
new definition: The first part of a talk that welcomes people and explains the topic.
old example: A strong introduction tells the audience who you are, what you'll cover, and how long it will take — giving everyone a reason to pay attention from the first minute.
new example: In her introduction, she explained the bike talk would last 30 minutes.

old definition: A structured list of topics you will cover, shared at the start of a presentation. Presenting the agenda upfront helps the audience follow along and shows that your time together is well organised.
new definition: A list of the topics that will be covered in a meeting or talk.
old example: The agenda covers four sections — the current challenge, the proposed solution, results from existing clients, and time for questions — so the audience knows exactly what to expect and when.
new example: He showed the agenda with four parts to the two women in the hotel lobby.

old definition: A word or phrase that guides the listener through the structure of a presentation — telling them where you are and where you are going. Common signposts: 'moving on to', 'as I mentioned', 'to summarise'.
new definition: A word or phrase that tells listeners where you are in a talk.
old example: A signpost like 'we're now in section two of three' tells the audience exactly where they are in the presentation — so they can follow along without losing track.
new example: She used a signpost to tell the two men they were in part two of three.

old definition: A phrase used to move smoothly from one section of a presentation to the next. Good transitions link ideas together and make the presentation feel natural rather than disconnected.
new definition: A change from one topic or section to the next one.
old example: A clean transition from the problem to the solution gives the audience a clear moment to shift focus — linking what they just heard to what is coming next.
new example: He made a smooth transition from the energy problem to the solar panel solution.

old definition: Extra importance or stress given to a point so the audience pays particular attention to it. You create emphasis by slowing down, repeating a key idea, or using phrases like 'the key point here is'.
new definition: Special importance or stress given to something so that people notice it.
old example: When a number is the most important point in a section, emphasis makes sure the audience doesn't miss it — pausing before the figure and naming it clearly is often enough.
new example: She put emphasis on the 30% figure by pointing at it on the screen.

old definition: A brief recap of the main points at the end of a presentation. A strong summary reminds the audience of what they heard, reinforces the key messages, and sets up the next step.
new definition: A short statement of the main points of something.
old example: A good summary at the end of a presentation pulls the key points together — the challenge, the solution, and the results — and gives the audience a clear picture before the next step.
new example: He gave the chefs a short summary of the three main points about food supply.

old definition: To capture and hold the audience's attention. A presenter who engages their audience asks questions, tells stories, and connects the content directly to the listener's experience.
new definition: To get people interested and keep their attention.
old example: When a presentation includes a live demonstration and invites questions throughout, the audience stays engaged rather than passively waiting for it to end.
new example: She engaged the visitors at the water filter stand by asking them a question.

old definition: The organised framework of a presentation — introduction, body, and conclusion. A clear structure helps the audience follow the content and remember the key messages after the presentation ends.
new definition: The way the parts of something are organised and fit together.
old example: A clear structure — an opening, an operational middle, and a defined goal at the end — makes it easy for the audience to follow the presentation from start to finish.
new example: She explained the structure of the warehouse plan to her three colleagues.

old definition: The standard professional opener for a presentation section or the whole presentation. 'Start by' introduces the first action — what you will do to begin. Always use 'by' followed by '-ing'.
new definition: A polite way to say what you will do first in a talk.
old example: I'd like to start by giving you a quick overview of the market context — so that when we get to the product, you'll already understand why the timing matters.
new example: I'd like to start by looking at the map of our coffee shop locations.

old definition: A clear, professional way to present the agenda. 'I'll be covering' uses the future continuous to signal that these topics will unfold over the course of the presentation.
new definition: A polite way to tell people the topics you will talk about.
old example: Today I'll be covering three things — the problem, the product, and the results — and each section builds on the last, so by the end you'll have a complete picture.
new example: Today I'll be covering the skin problem, our new serum, and the results.

old definition: The standard transition phrase for moving from one section to the next in a presentation. It is a signpost — it tells the audience they are now moving forward to new content.
new definition: A phrase used to change to the next topic.
old example: Moving on to how the system works in practice — now that we've established the challenge, let me show you how the solution addresses it step by step.
new example: Moving on to irrigation, let me show you how the system waters the vines.

old definition: A phrase used to signal the most important idea in a section. It tells the audience to pay close attention — this is the thing they should remember even if they forget everything else.
new definition: A phrase that introduces the most important idea.
old example: The key point here is that the platform doesn't just reduce workload — it turns a fragmented process into a consistent, repeatable experience the whole team can rely on.
new example: The key point here is that the new process is much simpler for the kitchen team.

old definition: The phrase that opens the closing section of a presentation. It signals that you are now recapping the main points — giving the audience a final, clear reminder of what they just heard.
new definition: A phrase used to begin a short list of the main points.
old example: To summarise — we've covered the market context, the challenge it creates, the growth opportunity, and the outcome you can expect — and I'd now like to open it up for questions.
new example: To summarise, the apartment tower has a great location, a strong design, and good returns.

word: I'D BE HAPPY TO TAKE ANY QUESTIONS
old definition: The professional phrase for opening the Q&A section after a presentation. 'Take' is the standard verb for questions in a presentation context — not 'answer' or 'receive'.
new definition: A polite way to invite the audience to ask questions after a talk.
old example: I'd be happy to take any questions now — on the product, the process, or anything from the presentation — before we move on to the next step.
new example: I'd be happy to take any questions about the cleaning robot now.

old definition: A real story about how a customer used your product to fix a problem and get good results.
new definition: A detailed report about a real customer and how a product helped them.
old example: A case study shows the full story — a business that was struggling with paper-based records and falling sales, and how the right solution turned that around into growth, happy customers, and a full checklist of results.
new example: The case study followed a café owner who replaced paper receipts with a tablet.

old definition: To start using a new system, plan, or product in your company.
new definition: To start using a new plan, system, or idea.
old example: Once the team was ready to implement the system, the entire process moved through four clear steps — setup, scanning, packaging, and dispatch — with every order confirmed and on its way at the end.
new example: She plans to implement the new scanning system across the whole warehouse.

old definition: The result of something — what happened in the end after a decision or action.
new definition: The result of an action, event, or decision.
old example: The outcome of using a smart irrigation system was a full crop cycle completed with less water and a higher yield — from sensor to harvest, every step connected, tracked, and feeding into a growing basket of results.
new example: She was happy with the outcome: healthier lettuce and more tomatoes to sell.

old definition: Something you can show with exact numbers, like percentages or hours saved.
new definition: Able to be counted or checked using numbers.
old example: Every improvement was measurable — response time cut almost in half, guest ratings up from 4.2 to 4.8, occupancy rising from 68% to 87%, and on-time check-in climbing from 72% to 94%.
new example: The hotel manager checked the measurable results on his tablet in the lobby.

old definition: Return on investment — the money or value you get back compared to what you spent.
new definition: Return on investment: the profit you get compared with the money you spent.
old example: The ROI of switching to an electric fleet was visible across the whole operation — fuel costs fell sharply, the savings compounded month on month, and delivery performance continued to improve across all 32 vehicles.
new example: She checked the ROI of the new electric vans on her tablet.

old definition: What a happy customer says about your product — their own words about their experience.
new definition: A statement from a customer saying they are happy with a product or service.
old example: A strong testimonial from a satisfied customer — with a verified five-star rating — carries more weight in a sales conversation than any claim the vendor could make themselves.
new example: The restaurant owner shared a five-star testimonial from a happy guest.

old definition: Keeping your customers so they continue to buy from you or stay with your company.
new definition: The ability to keep customers, members, or workers over a long time.
old example: Retention improved month on month for six consecutive months — members kept coming back, and the renewal curve rose steadily to a near-perfect result by the end of the period.
new example: The gym handed out renewal cards to members, and retention stayed high.

old definition: A big change that makes something work in a completely different and better way.
new definition: A complete change in how something looks or works.
old example: The transformation was visible in every part of the business — from a cramped workshop with manual processes to a modern studio with digital design tools, sustainable production, and a team finally working at full capacity.
new example: She walked proudly through the transformation of her old workshop into a modern studio.

word: ONE OF OUR CUSTOMERS WAS FACING...
old definition: Use this to start a success story and describe the problem a customer had before your solution.
new definition: A phrase that introduces a customer who had a certain problem.
old example: One of our customers was facing a scheduling problem — appointments were piling up, staff coordination was breaking down, and there was no system linking bookings to available capacity.
new example: One of our customers was facing scheduling problems at his dental clinic.

word: AFTER IMPLEMENTING OUR SOLUTION, THEY WERE ABLE TO...
old definition: Use this to show what a customer could do after they started using your product.
new definition: A phrase that says what became possible once the solution was in use.
old example: After implementing our solution, they were able to automate the entire tracking process — from activation to verification to routing — without a single manual intervention at any stage.
new example: After implementing our solution, they were able to sort luggage automatically at the airport.

word: WITHIN [TIME], THEY SAW A [PERCENTAGE] IMPROVEMENT IN...
old definition: Use this to share a specific result with a number and how quickly it happened.
new definition: A phrase that tells how fast a result happened and by how much.
old example: Within 90 days, they saw a 28% improvement in output — more handled per person, with fewer hours spent on each one, and the whole team operating at a pace they hadn't seen before.
new example: Within 90 days, they saw a 28% improvement in call centre productivity.

word: WHAT THIS MEANT FOR THEIR BUSINESS WAS...
old definition: Use this to explain why a result was important and what it changed for the customer.
new definition: A phrase that explains the effect a result had on a company.
old example: What this meant for their business was a chain reaction — faster delivery led to better quality checks, happier customer relationships, growing revenue, and eventually the opening of a second location.
new example: What this meant for their business was faster deliveries and a second showroom.

old definition: Use this to share what a customer said about your product in their own words.
new definition: A phrase used to report what a customer's manager said.
old example: Their manager told us that the team noticed the difference within the first week — and that the confidence it gave them in the equipment was something they hadn't expected going in.
new example: Their manager told us that the new process saves the repair team hours every day.

word: THAT'S EXACTLY THE KIND OF RESULT WE AIM TO DELIVER FOR EVERY CUSTOMER WE WORK WITH
old definition: Use this to close a success story and promise the same results to the person you are speaking with.
new definition: A phrase saying that this good result is what the company wants for all customers.
old example: Hotels, warehouses, retailers, clinics — consistent, measurable improvement with a checkmark at the end of every engagement. That's exactly the kind of result we aim to deliver for every customer we work with.
new example: Shorter waits and better ratings are exactly the kind of result we aim to deliver.

old definition: To discuss the conditions of a deal in order to reach an agreement that works for both sides.
new definition: To talk about the terms of a deal until both sides agree.
old example: Both sides agreed to negotiate the price before signing the contract.
new example: They will negotiate the terms of the contract before anyone picks up the pen.

old definition: An agreement where both sides give up something in order to reach a deal.
new definition: An agreement where both sides give up something to reach a deal.
old example: They reached a compromise — a lower price in exchange for a longer contract.
new example: She lowered her price and he ordered more fabric, which was a fair compromise.

old definition: A response to an offer that suggests different conditions instead of simply accepting or refusing.
new definition: An answer to an offer that suggests different terms instead of accepting or refusing.
old example: The client made a counter-offer of $28 per user instead of the original price of $35.
new example: He made a counter-offer of 3,820,000 after seeing the 4,150,000 price.

old definition: A polite way to suggest an alternative and ask if the other person is willing to consider it.
new definition: A polite way to suggest another option and ask if someone would consider it.
old example: Would you be open to a 12-month contract in exchange for a lower monthly rate?
new example: Would you be open to seeing our fabric samples in our showroom today?

word: IF WE WERE ABLE TO [X], WOULD YOU BE ABLE TO [Y]?
old definition: A formal way to propose an exchange — if we change one thing, would you agree to change something in return?
new definition: A formal way to suggest a trade: if we change one thing, will you change another?
old example: If we were able to shorten the onboarding to one month, would you be able to agree to the $28 rate?
new example: If we were able to ship earlier, would you be able to order more boards?

word: THAT'S AT THE VERY EDGE OF WHAT WE CAN OFFER
old definition: Used to say that this is close to the lowest price or best offer you are able to make.
new definition: Used to say this is nearly the lowest price or best deal we can give.
old example: $28 per user is at the very edge of what we can offer — any lower and we would need to adjust the package.
new example: That's at the very edge of what we can offer, as the gauge shows.

word: I THINK WE'RE CLOSE — LET'S SEE IF WE CAN FIND A MIDDLE GROUND
old definition: Used when both sides are nearly in agreement and you want to reach a final compromise.
new definition: Used when both sides are almost in agreement and want to find a fair compromise.
old example: I think we're close on price — let's see if we can find a middle ground on the payment terms.
new example: I think we're close, let's see if we can find a middle ground on delivery.

word: LET ME TAKE THAT BACK TO MY MANAGER AND COME BACK TO YOU
old definition: Used to say that you need to check internally before giving a final answer.
new definition: Used to say you must check with your boss before you give a final answer.
old example: Let me take that back to my manager and come back to you by end of day tomorrow.
new example: Let me take that back to my manager and come back to you tomorrow.

old definition: To bring a sales conversation to completion — when the buyer agrees to move forward. To close a deal means to win the customer's commitment.
new definition: To finish a sale when the customer agrees to buy.
old example: The sales team closed three deals in the last week of the quarter.
new example: The two managers shook hands over the contract and closed the deal.

old definition: An agreement or promise to move forward. A commitment can be a signed contract or just an agreed next step with a clear timeline.
new definition: A promise or agreement to do something.
old example: The customer gave a commitment to sign the contract once the finance team confirmed the budget.
new example: He pressed a wax seal on the envelope, a commitment to deliver by the 18th.

old definition: A concern or reason the buyer gives for not moving forward yet. Objections often mean the buyer is still interested but has a final question that needs answering.
new definition: A reason someone gives for not agreeing to something yet.
old example: The customer raised an objection about the data processing agreement before agreeing to sign.
new example: She raised one objection and asked a question about the contract before signing.

old definition: A soft question used to check if the buyer is ready to commit — before asking for the formal close. It helps the salesperson understand how the buyer is feeling without pressure.
new definition: A gentle question that checks if someone is ready to decide.
old example: A trial close helps you understand how the buyer is feeling before asking for their final decision.
new example: The woman smiled, used a trial close, and reached her hand across the table.

old definition: A real reason for the buyer to decide now rather than later. Good urgency helps the buyer understand the cost of waiting — it does not pressure them into a bad decision.
new definition: The feeling that something must be done very soon.
old example: The price increase created urgency and pushed the client to sign before the deadline.
new example: He watched the hourglass and felt the urgency of the deadline on the 18th.

old definition: When a buyer delays making a decision without giving a clear reason. Stalling usually means there is an unspoken concern that needs to be discovered.
new definition: To stop making progress or delay, or for an engine to suddenly stop.
old example: The deal stalled for three weeks because the client could not get budget approval.
new example: His car stalled on the wet road, so he checked his phone.

old definition: The agreed action after a sales conversation — who will do what, and by when. A clear next step turns a verbal yes into a concrete plan.
new definition: The action that will happen after a meeting or conversation.
old example: The agreed next step was to send the contract today and confirm by Friday.
new example: She stepped onto the next stone while her colleague smiled and watched.

old definition: In the assumptive close, the salesperson acts as if the buyer has already decided to move forward. It feels confident and makes it easier for the buyer to say yes.
new definition: Acting as if something is already true or already decided.
old example: An assumptive close works by acting as if the buyer has already decided to move forward.
new example: She pointed to the signature line with her pen, assuming he had already agreed.

old definition: A confident, professional way to ask the buyer to commit. 'Shall we' is softer than 'Will you' — it implies a shared decision, not a demand. Always follow it with the specific next step.
new definition: A polite question asking if people are ready to continue together.
old example: Shall we move forward? I can have the contract ready to send today.
new example: Shall we move forward with this contract?

word: BASED ON EVERYTHING WE'VE COVERED, HOW ARE YOU FEELING?
old definition: A trial close phrase that invites the buyer to share how they feel before you ask for the commitment. 'How are you feeling?' is more open and less pressured than 'Are you ready?'
new definition: A question asking someone for their opinion after a discussion.
old example: Based on everything we've covered, how are you feeling about moving forward?
new example: Based on everything we've covered, how are you feeling about the plans on the table?

word: IS THERE ANYTHING STILL HOLDING YOU BACK?
old definition: A phrase for uncovering final concerns before the close. It sounds natural and non-confrontational — it implies the buyer wants to move forward but something is stopping them.
new definition: A question asking if something is stopping someone from deciding or acting.
old example: Is there anything still holding you back from moving forward today?
new example: Is there anything still holding you back from leaving the harbour?

word: WHAT WOULD NEED TO BE TRUE FOR YOU TO FEEL CONFIDENT MOVING FORWARD?
old definition: A question for when the buyer is vague about their hesitation. It asks them to say exactly what is missing so the salesperson can address it directly.
new definition: A question asking what conditions someone needs before they feel sure about continuing.
old example: What would need to be true for you to feel confident moving forward this week?
new example: What would need to be true for you to feel confident moving forward with this project?

word: IF YOU'RE HAPPY WITH EVERYTHING, I CAN SEND THE CONTRACT TODAY
old definition: A phrase that moves from checking satisfaction to proposing action. 'If you are happy' is low-pressure. 'I can send the contract today' creates gentle urgency without demanding an immediate signature.
new definition: A polite way to offer to send the contract if the other person agrees.
old example: If you're happy with everything, I can send the contract today so your team has time to review it.
new example: If you're happy with everything, I can send the contract today.

old definition: A phrase that turns a verbal yes into a concrete plan. Use it at the end of every sales call — always close with a specific action, an owner, and a date.
new definition: A phrase used to decide together what will happen next.
old example: Let's agree on next steps — I'll send the contract today and follow up on Friday.
new example: Let's agree on next steps and put a name and a date on each task.

old definition: The rate at which customers stop buying from a company or cancel their subscription. High churn means the company is losing customers.
new definition: The rate at which customers stop buying or cancel their subscription.
old example: The company has a high churn rate because customers are cancelling after the first 90 days.
new example: She looked at the cancelled accounts on her screens and worried about the high churn.

old definition: Net Promoter Score — a number that shows how loyal customers are. Customers rate from 0 to 10 how likely they are to recommend the company to a friend. Abbreviated as NPS.
new definition: A score that shows how likely customers are to recommend a company to others.
old example: The company's NPS is 34, which means there is still work to do to improve customer loyalty.
new example: He looked at the NPS survey on his tablet and at the chart on the wall.

old definition: A system that rewards customers for buying again — through points, discounts, or special access. It gives customers a reason to choose you instead of a competitor.
new definition: A system that gives rewards to customers who keep buying from a company.
old example: The loyalty programme gives long-term customers early access to new products and a dedicated account manager.
new example: He handed her a black envelope with details of her new loyalty programme membership.

old definition: The total amount of money a company expects to earn from one customer over the whole time they stay. Also called LTV.
new definition: The total money a company expects to earn from one customer over time.
old example: The average lifetime value of a customer is £4,200, so keeping customers longer has a big impact on revenue.
new example: She showed the group that strategic customers have the highest lifetime value.

old definition: The process of reconnecting with customers who have stopped buying or using the product — to bring them back before they leave completely.
new definition: Contacting customers who have stopped buying to get them interested again.
old example: A re-engagement campaign was sent to customers who had not opened an email in three months.
new example: She smiled at the re-engagement email on her phone offering 25% off her next order.

old definition: The percentage of customers who continue to buy from a company over a period of time. A higher retention rate means more customers are staying.
new definition: The percentage of customers who keep buying from a company over time.
old example: The 12-month retention rate improved from 61% to 70% after the new onboarding programme was launched.
new example: She showed her team that the retention rate is much higher after the changes.

old definition: A campaign to bring back customers who have already cancelled or stopped buying. Unlike re-engagement, win-back targets customers who have already left.
new definition: An effort to get customers who have already left to come back.
old example: A win-back campaign was sent to customers who cancelled in the last 12 months, showing them what had changed.
new example: He read the win-back email on his laptop and thought about returning.

old definition: The process of helping new customers get started and reach their first result quickly. Good onboarding makes customers much less likely to leave.
new definition: The process of helping new customers get started with a product or service.
old example: The company redesigned its onboarding to help new customers see results in their first week.
new example: She smiled and raised her fist when she finished the last step of onboarding.

word: WE NEED TO REDUCE CHURN BY...
old definition: A phrase for setting a specific target to lose fewer customers. Always include a number — a percentage, a number of customers, or a revenue amount.
new definition: A phrase used to say how many fewer customers the company must lose.
old example: We need to reduce churn by 1.5 percentage points by the end of Q4.
new example: We need to reduce churn by two percent before the end of Q4.

word: THE LIFETIME VALUE OF THIS CUSTOMER SEGMENT IS...
old definition: A phrase for presenting the total revenue expected from a specific group of customers. Always give a specific number.
new definition: A phrase used to tell people how much money one group of customers brings.
old example: The lifetime value of the enterprise customer segment is approximately £18,000.
new example: The lifetime value of this customer segment is about £20,000 per customer.

word: WE SHOULD RUN A RE-ENGAGEMENT CAMPAIGN FOR...
old definition: A phrase for proposing a campaign to reconnect with inactive customers. Always say who the campaign is for and why they are at risk.
new definition: A phrase used to suggest contacting customers who have stopped using the product.
old example: We should run a re-engagement campaign for customers who have not logged in for 45 days.
new example: We should run a re-engagement campaign for customers who have been inactive for more than 45 days.

old definition: A phrase for sharing a specific insight from Net Promoter Score data. Always follow with a clear finding — a score, a trend, or a pattern.
new definition: A phrase used to share what the customer score results tell us.
old example: Our NPS shows that customers who complete the full onboarding programme are much more likely to stay.
new example: Our NPS shows that most customers are happy, but some are still unhappy.

word: THE LOYALTY PROGRAMME IS DESIGNED TO...
old definition: A phrase for explaining the purpose of a loyalty programme — what behaviour it encourages and what result it will deliver for the business.
new definition: A phrase used to explain the purpose of a loyalty programme.
old example: The loyalty programme is designed to increase purchase frequency and turn satisfied customers into referrers.
new example: The loyalty programme is designed to reward shoppers and encourage them to tell their friends.

word: WE ARE TARGETING A RETENTION RATE OF...
old definition: A phrase for stating a specific retention goal. Always give the percentage and the timeframe.
new definition: A phrase used to state the retention goal a company wants to reach.
old example: We are targeting a retention rate of 78% at 12 months, up from 61% currently.
new example: We are targeting a retention rate of 85% within the next 12 months.

old definition: To value what someone did and feel thankful for it.
new definition: To feel thankful for something someone did.
old example: We really appreciate your help.
new example: We really appreciate your order.

old definition: Feeling thankful for something someone did for you.
new definition: Feeling thankful for something someone did for you.
old example: I am very grateful for your help.
new example: I am very grateful for your order.

old definition: Important to you, and treated with care and respect.
new definition: Important to you and treated with care and respect.
old example: You are a valued customer.
new example: You are a valued customer.

old definition: A happy feeling you get from doing something good or nice.
new definition: A happy feeling you get from doing something nice.
old example: It was a pleasure to meet you.
new example: It was a pleasure to help you today.

old definition: Comments about something, to say what is good or bad.
new definition: Comments that say what is good or bad about something.
old example: Please give us feedback on our service.
new example: Please give us feedback on our service.

old definition: To tell others that something is good and they should try it.
new definition: To tell someone that something is good and they should try it.
old example: I recommend this restaurant. The food is great.
new example: I recommend the Pro plan. It is our most popular one.

old definition: The happy feeling when something is good and you get what you want.
new definition: The happy feeling when you get what you want.
old example: Your satisfaction is very important to us.
new example: Your satisfaction is very important to us.

old definition: Staying with the same company or person for a long time.
new definition: Staying with the same company or person for a long time.
old example: We thank you for your loyalty.
new example: We thank you for your loyalty.

old definition: A polite thing to say to a customer after they buy something.
new definition: A polite thing to say to a customer after they buy something.
old example: Thank you for your order. It will arrive on Monday.
new example: Thank you for your order. It will arrive on Monday.

word: IT WAS A PLEASURE WORKING WITH YOU
old definition: A polite way to say you enjoyed working with someone.
new definition: A polite way to say you enjoyed working with someone.
old example: Goodbye, and thank you. It was a pleasure working with you.
new example: Thank you for the order. It was a pleasure working with you.

word: PLEASE DO NOT HESITATE TO CONTACT US
old definition: A polite way to say: ask us anytime, do not wait.
new definition: A polite way to say you can ask us at any time.
old example: If you have questions, please do not hesitate to contact us.
new example: If you have questions, please do not hesitate to contact us.

old definition: A polite way to thank a customer for buying from you.
new definition: A polite way to thank a customer for buying from you.
old example: Thank you for coming. We appreciate your business.
new example: Thank you for coming. We appreciate your business.

word: I HOPE YOU ARE HAPPY WITH YOUR [PRODUCT]
old definition: A kind way to ask if a customer likes what they bought.
new definition: A kind way to ask if a customer likes what they bought.
old example: I hope you are happy with your new phone.
new example: I hope you are happy with your new phone.

word: WE LOOK FORWARD TO WORKING WITH YOU AGAIN
old definition: A polite way to say you want to work together again.
new definition: A polite way to say you want to work together again.
old example: Thank you for today. We look forward to working with you again.
new example: Thank you for today. We look forward to working with you again.

old definition: To look at two things together to see how they are the same or different.
new definition: To look at two things to see how they are the same or different.
old example: Let me compare the two phones before I buy one.
new example: Let me compare these two laptops for you.

old definition: A special part of a product that makes it useful.
new definition: A special part of a product that makes it useful.
old example: This phone has a great camera feature.
new example: This calendar has a sync feature for your whole team.

old definition: Not too expensive, so most people can pay for it.
new definition: Not too expensive, so most people can pay for it.
old example: This hotel is nice and affordable.
new example: This laptop is nice and affordable.

old definition: Liked by many people.
new definition: Liked by many people.
old example: Pizza is a very popular food.
new example: This game is very popular with our customers.

old definition: Having more features or better technology than a simple one.
new definition: Having more features or better technology than a simple one.
old example: This is an advanced phone with many extra tools.
new example: This advanced model has many extra tools.

old definition: Simple, with no extra parts.
new definition: Simple, with no extra parts.
old example: I only need a basic phone for calls.
new example: The basic plan has only calls and texts.

old definition: Right for a certain person or situation.
new definition: Right for a certain person or situation.
old example: This bag is well suited for school.
new example: This laptop is well suited for your team.

old definition: To change to a better or newer version.
new definition: To change to a better or newer version.
old example: I want to upgrade my phone this year.
new example: Do you want to upgrade your armor to level 3?

word: THIS ONE IS [ADJECTIVE]-ER THAN THAT ONE
old definition: Use this to compare two things with short adjectives by adding -er.
new definition: Use this to compare two things with short adjectives by adding -er.
old example: This bike is cheaper than that one.
new example: This laptop is cheaper than that one.

word: THIS ONE IS MORE [ADJECTIVE] THAN THAT ONE
old definition: Use this to compare two things with longer adjectives by adding more.
new definition: Use this to compare two things with longer adjectives by adding more.
old example: This phone is more popular than that one.
new example: This phone is more popular than that one.

old definition: Use this to tell the most important way two things are not the same.
new definition: Use this to tell the most important way two things are not the same.
old example: The main difference is the price.
new example: The main difference is the price.

old definition: Use this to say what two things both have.
new definition: Use this to say what two things both have.
old example: Both plans include free delivery.
new example: Both plans include free delivery.

word: IF YOU WANT [BENEFIT], THIS ONE IS BETTER
old definition: Use this to match what a person wants with the best choice.
new definition: Use this to match what a person wants with the best choice.
old example: If you want a big screen, this one is better.
new example: If you want a big screen, this one is better.

word: FOR YOUR TEAM, I WOULD RECOMMEND
old definition: Use this to give your final advice to someone.
new definition: Use this to give your final advice to someone.
old example: For your team, I would recommend the red one.
new example: For your team, I would recommend the blue one.

old definition: A person or company that has shown early interest in what you sell.
new definition: A person or company that has shown early interest in what you sell.
old example: He checked the new lead, who had visited the website and downloaded resources.
new example: He checked the new lead, who had visited the website and downloaded resources.

old definition: A potential customer who is likely to buy.
new definition: A person or company that might buy from you soon.
old example: He met the prospect, who had the budget, the need, and the authority.
new example: This prospect has the budget, the need, and the authority to decide.

old definition: A short presentation that tries to persuade people to buy something.
new definition: A short talk that tries to persuade people to buy something.
old example: He gave his pitch about the new laptop to the people around the table.
new example: His pitch about the new laptop impressed everyone at the table.

old definition: Contact you make after a meeting to continue the conversation.
new definition: Contact you make after a meeting to continue the conversation.
old example: She made a follow-up call after sending the proposal.
new example: She made a follow-up call after sending the proposal.

old definition: To complete a sale when the customer agrees to buy.
new definition: To complete a sale when the customer agrees to buy.
old example: She smiled and shook his hand to close the sale.
new example: She smiled and shook his hand after they managed to close the sale.

old definition: All the deals a company is working on, at different stages.
new definition: All the deals a company is working on, at different stages.
old example: Our pipeline has five stages, from prospect to closed.
new example: Our pipeline has five stages, from prospect to closed.

old definition: To check if a lead is suitable to become a customer.
new definition: To check if a lead is suitable to become a customer.
old example: She used her laptop to qualify the lead by checking budget, need, and authority.
new example: She will qualify this lead by checking the budget, need, and authority.

old definition: To help a relationship grow by giving regular care and attention.
new definition: To help a business relationship grow by staying in regular contact.
old example: He wants to nurture this contact, so he meets her for coffee.
new example: He wants to nurture this contact, so he invited her for coffee.

old definition: To go from one stage of a process to the next.
new definition: To go from one stage of a sale to the next.
old example: The deal is moving through the pipeline and is now at the proposal stage.
new example: The deal is moving through the pipeline and is now at the proposal stage.

old definition: To check if a lead is a good match to become a customer.
new definition: To check if a lead is a good match to become a customer.
old example: We qualified a lead after checking its budget, need, and authority.
new example: We qualified a lead after checking its budget, need, and authority.

old definition: To finish the final agreement with a customer.
new definition: To finish the final agreement with a customer.
old example: After the proposal and negotiation, they were able to close a deal.
new example: After the proposal and negotiation, we were finally able to close the deal.

old definition: To contact someone again about something discussed earlier.
new definition: To contact someone again about something discussed earlier.
old example: She is following up on the proposal with a phone call.
new example: She is following up on the proposal with a phone call.

old definition: A question that asks which step something has reached in a process.
new definition: A question that asks which step something has reached in a process.
old example: At what stage is the Acme Corp deal for $120,000?
new example: At what stage is the Acme Corp deal for $120,000?

old definition: To present a product or idea to someone to persuade them.
new definition: To present a product or idea to someone to persuade them.
old example: He pitches to the older man, showing a smart solution on the screen.
new example: He is pitching to the client about how the solution reduces costs.

old definition: The first part of a call or talk, when you greet someone and begin.
new definition: The first part of a call or meeting, when you greet people and begin.
old example: He smiles at the camera and gives a friendly opening to the video call.
new example: Thanks for your time today. I'm excited to connect with you.

old definition: The reason why you do something or why you call someone.
new definition: The reason why you do something or why you call someone.
old example: He explains the purpose of the call while he types on his laptop.
new example: The purpose of my call is to understand your current challenges.

old definition: A list of the things that will be discussed in a meeting or call.
new definition: A list of the things that will be discussed in a meeting or call.
old example: He looks at the agenda on his laptop while he talks on the phone.
new example: Our agenda has four points: introduction, goals, solution overview and next steps.

old definition: A friendly relationship where people understand each other and feel comfortable.
new definition: A friendly relationship where people understand each other and feel comfortable.
old example: The two men smile and talk easily, so they already have good rapport.
new example: We built good rapport quickly because we both enjoy the same sport.

old definition: A reason you give for disagreeing with something or not wanting it.
new definition: A reason you give for disagreeing with something or not wanting it.
old example: He has an objection about the price and explains his worry to the other man.
new example: My main objection is the price, and I also worry about the time.

old definition: A promise or agreement to do something.
new definition: A promise or agreement to do something.
old example: She smiles and points to the next step, hoping for a commitment.
new example: Are you ready to make a commitment and schedule the next step?

old definition: To move from one part of a conversation or activity to the next.
new definition: To move from one part of a conversation to the next.
old example: She smiles at the man and begins to transition to the next topic.
new example: Now that we've covered that, let me transition to the solution.

old definition: To repeat the main points of something in a short way.
new definition: To repeat the main points of something in a short way.
old example: She smiles at her laptop and recaps the three key points of the meeting.
new example: Let me recap the three key points before we choose a next step.

word: THE REASON FOR MY CALL IS
old definition: A phrase you use at the start of a call to say why you are calling.
new definition: A phrase you use at the start of a call to say why you are calling.
old example: The reason for my call is to confirm our meeting on Thursday afternoon.
new example: The reason for my call is to review your pipeline for this quarter.

old definition: A phrase you use to say something first, before the main discussion starts.
new definition: A phrase you use to say something first, before the main discussion starts.
old example: Before we dive in, would you like some water or a coffee?
new example: Before we dive in, let me quickly explain how today's meeting will work.

old definition: A polite phrase used to begin asking someone a question about a topic.
new definition: A polite phrase used to begin asking someone a question about a topic.
old example: Can I ask you about your team and how you work now?
new example: Can I ask you about your current setup and your team?

word: BASED ON WHAT YOU'VE TOLD ME
old definition: A phrase meaning you are using the information that someone gave you.
new definition: A phrase meaning you are using the information that someone gave you.
old example: Based on what you've told me, this plan should help your company grow.
new example: Based on what you've told me, this strategy should help you improve your ROI.

word: WHAT I'D LIKE TO PROPOSE IS
old definition: A polite phrase used to introduce a suggestion or plan.
new definition: A polite phrase used to introduce a suggestion or plan.
old example: What I'd like to propose is a new plan with ongoing support.

old example: Asking 'how long have you been managing this without a proper system?' does not say the current situation is a problem — but the implication is clear, and it is more powerful because the prospect draws that conclusion themselves.
new example: The implication of her question was that the current system was failing.

old definition: Placing two options, situations, or outcomes side by side so the difference between them becomes obvious and one feels like the clear choice.
new definition: Showing two things side by side so the difference between them is clear.
old example: Contrast is one of the most powerful tools in persuasion — 'you are currently spending fifteen hours a week on something this tool does in twenty minutes' is not an argument, it is a contrast. The conclusion makes itself.
new example: The contrast between twenty minutes and fifteen hours made the client pause.

old definition: The trust and authority that makes people believe what you say — built through specificity, honesty, and occasionally conceding a point that goes against you.
new definition: The quality of being trusted and believed by other people.
old example: Credibility is not built by being impressive — it is built by being accurate. One honest admission ('this is not the right fit if you only have five reps') does more for your credibility than ten strong claims.
new example: Admitting the product's limits gave her real credibility with the buyer.

old definition: To acknowledge a point the other person has made — even one that works against you. A counterintuitive move that builds trust faster than defending every position.
new definition: To admit that a point someone made is true, even if it hurts you.
old example: If a prospect says your onboarding takes longer than a competitor's and they are right, concede it immediately — then explain what you get in return for that time. Trying to argue against a true point destroys credibility.
new example: I will concede that our onboarding takes longer than our competitor's.

old definition: Introduce your frame explicitly — signals that you are about to offer a perspective, not just present a fact. Invites the listener in rather than imposing.
new definition: A phrase used to introduce your own opinion or view of a situation.
old example: The way I see it, the question is not whether you need better pipeline visibility — you have already told me you do. The question is whether the cost of not fixing it is greater than the cost of fixing it. I think it clearly is.
new example: The way I see it, this delay is costing your team more.

word: WHAT THIS REALLY COMES DOWN TO IS
old definition: Strip away complexity and name the single core issue — a reframing move that refocuses the conversation when it has drifted or become too complicated.
new definition: A phrase used to name the single most important point in a discussion.
old example: We can talk about features all day, but what this really comes down to is one question: can your team afford to keep losing two or three deals a month to a problem that is entirely fixable?
new example: What this really comes down to is whether your team can trust the data.

old definition: Offer an analogy or new angle to help the prospect see their situation differently — useful when the current frame is blocking them from making a decision.
new definition: A phrase used to introduce a comparison that helps someone see things differently.
old example: Think of it this way — you would not run a finance team without accounting software, even though spreadsheets technically work. At some point, 'it technically works' stops being a good reason to keep doing something manually.
new example: Think of it this way: the software pays for itself within one quarter.

word: THE QUESTION IS NOT — IT IS
old definition: Explicitly reject one frame and replace it with a better one — one of the most direct repositioning moves in a sales conversation.
new definition: A structure that rejects one way of seeing an issue and offers another.
old example: The question is not whether Brightline is expensive relative to the alternatives. The question is whether the deals you are losing every month cost more than the tool. They do — by a significant margin.
new example: The question is not what it costs; it is what waiting costs.

word: WHAT MOST PEOPLE IN YOUR POSITION FIND IS
old definition: Use light social proof to make the direction you are suggesting feel normal and validated — reduces the sense that they are being asked to take a risk.
new definition: A phrase that uses what similar people experience to make a suggestion feel normal.
old example: What most Sales VPs in your position find is that the visibility problem is not actually about the reps — it is about the system. Once you change the system, the behaviour follows.
new example: What most directors in your position find is that adoption improves within weeks.

word: LET ME BE DIRECT ABOUT SOMETHING
old definition: Signal that you are about to say something honest and possibly uncomfortable — builds credibility and disarms defensiveness before you say the thing.
new definition: A phrase that signals you are about to say something honest and blunt.
old example: Let me be direct about something — if your team has not adopted a tool in three attempts, the issue is probably not the tools. That is worth understanding before you invest in another one.
new example: Let me be direct about something: the proposed timeline is unrealistic.

old definition: To identify the root cause of a problem by asking questions and listening carefully — before suggesting any solution. The word comes from medicine, and the parallel is intentional.
new definition: To find the real cause of a problem by asking questions and listening.
old example: The mistake most salespeople make is that they start recommending before they have done the work to diagnose — so they end up pitching solutions to symptoms rather than causes.
new example: She needs to diagnose the issue before she recommends anything to the client.

old definition: To ask a follow-up question that goes deeper than the surface answer — the move that separates consultative sellers from people who just listen politely.
new definition: To ask a deeper follow-up question to learn more about something.
old example: When James said 'we have a reporting problem', most salespeople would have started pitching reporting features. Riley probed instead: 'What does a reporting problem actually cost you in a typical week?'
new example: Let me probe a little further on what changed last quarter.

old definition: Describing the real or hidden cause beneath what someone first says — the thing beneath the thing. Prospects often describe symptoms; the underlying issue is what needs addressing.
new definition: Describing the hidden or real cause that lies beneath the obvious problem.
old example: The stated problem was slow reporting. The underlying issue was that no one trusted the data — so even fast reports would not have fixed anything.
new example: The underlying issue is that the team never agreed on clear criteria.

old definition: Something you believe to be true about a prospect's situation without having checked — the enemy of consultative selling. Good discovery replaces assumptions with evidence.
new definition: Something you accept as true without having checked the facts.
old example: Going into the call, Riley had assumed the team's main problem was pipeline visibility. That assumption was wrong — the real issue was data quality upstream of the pipeline.
new example: I went into the meeting with an assumption that budget was the issue.

old definition: To determine whether a prospect's situation is a genuine fit for what you offer — and just as importantly, to recognise when it is not. Consultative sellers qualify honestly.
new definition: To decide whether a prospect is a genuine fit for what you offer.
old example: After twenty minutes of discovery, Riley realised the prospect needed a data integration tool before they needed Brightline. She said so — and qualified them out. They came back six months later.
new example: She spent ten minutes trying to qualify the lead on budget, need and authority.

old definition: To express a need, problem, or goal clearly and precisely in words. Many prospects can feel a problem but struggle to articulate it — helping them do that is one of the most valuable things a consultative seller does.
new definition: To express an idea, need or problem clearly in words.
old example: James had been frustrated with his team's performance for months but had not been able to articulate why. The discovery call helped him see that the problem was process, not people.
new example: Many clients struggle to articulate exactly what is going wrong.

old definition: What matters most to the prospect right now — not what is on their list, but what is at the top of it. Consultative sellers always establish priorities before making any recommendation.
new definition: The thing that matters most and deserves attention first.
old example: James listed four problems in the first five minutes. Riley did not respond to any of them immediately — she asked him to rank them by priority first, then focused the rest of the call on the top two.
new example: Cutting delivery times is our top priority for this project.

old definition: A specific condition or standard the solution must meet — understanding the prospect's criteria early prevents you from presenting something that fails on a requirement you never knew about.
new definition: A standard or condition that something must meet.
old example: One of James's criteria was that any new tool had to integrate with their existing CRM without a custom build. Riley discovered this in minute eight — which saved both of them forty minutes of the wrong conversation.
new example: Integration with our current system is one criterion for the new tool.

old definition: Signals consultative intent from the opening — tells the prospect you are not going to pitch immediately, that you want to understand first. Sets the tone for the whole call.
new definition: A phrase used to say you want to understand the situation first.
old example: Before I suggest anything, I want to spend the first twenty minutes understanding what is actually happening in your team — because I have found that what people tell me at the start and what is really going on are often quite different.
new example: Before I suggest anything, could you walk me through your current process?

old definition: A soft entry into a deeper question — less confrontational than 'why' but more purposeful than 'tell me more'. Signals that you are genuinely curious rather than following a script.
new definition: A polite request for the other person to explain something in more detail.
old example: You mentioned that deals are slipping in the final stage. Help me understand what that looks like in practice — is it a price conversation, a timing issue, or something else entirely?
new example: Help me understand why the last rollout stalled in the second month.

word: WHAT DOES THAT LOOK LIKE IN PRACTICE
old definition: Turns a vague or abstract statement into a specific, observable situation — grounds the conversation in reality so you are working with evidence, not assumptions.
new definition: A question asking for a concrete, real-life example of something vague.
old example: You said the team is not following the process. What does that look like in practice — are they skipping steps, recording things late, or doing something different entirely from what the process requires?
new example: You said communication is poor, so what does that look like in practice?

word: WHAT WOULD A GOOD OUTCOME LOOK LIKE
old definition: Moves the conversation from problem to aspiration — essential before any recommendation, because it tells you what success means to this specific prospect.
new definition: A question asking the other person to describe the result they want.
old example: We have spent some time on what is not working. What would a good outcome look like for you six months from now — not the tool you use to get there, but the actual situation you want to be in?
new example: What would a good outcome look like for your team by the end of the year?

word: IF YOU HAD TO RANK THOSE
old definition: A prioritisation move that cuts through a list of problems and tells you what matters most — prevents you from responding to the wrong thing or treating everything as equally urgent.
new definition: A phrase asking someone to put several things in order of importance.
old example: You have mentioned three or four issues there. If you had to rank those by the one that is costing you the most right now — either in time, money, or deals — which would be at the top?
new example: If you had to rank those, which problem would come first?

old definition: A checking and confirming move that shows you have been listening actively and gives the prospect a chance to correct your understanding before you move to a recommendation.
new definition: A question that checks whether you have understood someone correctly.
old example: So the data goes in, but by the time it reaches the report it has been touched by three different people and no one is sure if the numbers are accurate. Am I reading this right — the problem is not the volume of data, it is the integrity?
new example: So the delays start in procurement. Am I reading this right?

old definition: The ability to say exactly what needs to be said in as few words as possible. In executive conversations, brevity is not just a style preference — it signals that you understand how decisions are made at that level.
new definition: Saying what you need to say using very few words.
old example: Riley had prepared thirty slides. She brought three. The brevity of her presentation was itself a signal that she understood how Sarah's day worked — and Sarah noticed.
new example: She kept her pitch short, and the CEO appreciated the brevity.

old definition: The specific goal or outcome an executive has been tasked with delivering — what they are personally accountable for. Understanding someone's mandate tells you what they actually care about.
new definition: The specific goal or result that a person has been given responsibility for.
old example: Sarah's mandate for the year was clear: reduce customer acquisition cost by 20% while maintaining revenue growth. Once Riley understood the mandate, she stopped talking about features and started talking about cost per deal.
new example: Your mandate is to cut acquisition costs by twenty percent this year.

old definition: A situation where improving one outcome requires accepting a cost or limitation in another — the language of executive decision-making. Executives make trade-off decisions constantly.
new definition: A situation where gaining one thing means accepting a loss in another.
old example: The trade-off Sarah was facing was real: she could invest in more headcount or in better tooling — but not both within the current budget. Riley's job was to make the tooling side of that trade-off as clear as possible.
new example: The trade-off is a higher monthly cost for much faster results.

old definition: Responsibility for delivering specific results — what executives are measured on and what keeps them up at night. Connecting your offer to an executive's accountability is the most reliable way to make it relevant.
new definition: Being responsible for results and having to explain them to others.
old example: Riley had done her research: Sarah had accountability for the full revenue number, not just new business. That meant efficiency across the whole funnel mattered — not just pipeline generation.
new example: As head of sales, you carry accountability for the whole revenue number.

old definition: The degree to which what you are proposing connects directly to the executive's current priorities and direction. Without alignment, even a good offer sounds like noise.
new definition: Agreement or close fit between two sets of goals or plans.
old example: The reason Riley's proposal landed well was not the product — it was the alignment. She had framed everything around the two outcomes Sarah had publicly stated as her priorities for the year.
new example: This proposal shows strong alignment with your priorities for the year.

old definition: To use a resource, relationship, data point, or insight to produce maximum effect — more than would be possible without it. Executives think in terms of leverage constantly.
new definition: To use something you already have to get a much bigger result.
old example: Riley offered to leverage the existing CRM data to generate a baseline in week one — which meant Sarah would see a real number within five days, not a projected one in thirty.
new example: We can leverage your existing CRM data to build a baseline quickly.

old definition: Anything that slows down a decision, creates unnecessary complexity, or adds resistance to a process. Executives have very little patience for friction — in decisions or in conversations.
new definition: Anything that slows a process down or makes it harder to complete.
old example: The previous vendor had created so much friction in the onboarding process that the team had abandoned the tool within sixty days. Riley made friction reduction the centrepiece of her implementation pitch.
new example: Three approval steps create real friction before any contract gets signed.

old definition: A meaningful piece of information that indicates what is really happening beneath the surface — as opposed to noise. Executives pay attention to signals and ignore most of the rest.
new definition: A meaningful piece of information that shows what is really going on.
old example: The fact that three of Sarah's top five reps had missed quota two quarters in a row was not a coincidence — it was a signal. Riley used that signal to open the conversation rather than starting with a product overview.
new example: Your top reps missing quota two quarters running is a clear signal.

old definition: Start with your conclusion, not your build-up — the way a newspaper headline tells you the story before you read the article. The single most important discipline in executive communication.
new definition: A phrase used to state your main conclusion before giving any details.
old example: The headline is this: your top five reps are closing at half the rate of the rest of the team, and the gap is entirely explainable — and fixable. I want to show you why in the next ten minutes.
new example: The headline is that your top reps are now closing less than before.

old definition: Explicitly connects a data point, observation, or claim to the executive's specific situation — removes the burden of translation from them and shows you have done the work to make it relevant.
new definition: A phrase used to link a fact directly to the listener's own situation.
old example: Churn in the B2B software sector is up 18% year on year. What this means for you is that your retention numbers from last year are no longer a reliable benchmark — the market has moved underneath them.
new example: Churn is up eighteen percent, and what this means for you is a tougher year.

word: THE RISK OF NOT ACTING IS
old definition: Frames the cost of inaction rather than the benefit of action — more powerful in executive conversations because executives are often more motivated by risk than by upside.
new definition: A phrase used to introduce the cost or danger of doing nothing.
old example: The risk of not acting on this before Q3 is that your competitor — who signed with us in January — will have six months of improved conversion data before your team starts. That gap compounds.
new example: The risk of not acting is that your competitor gets a six month head start.

word: WHERE DO YOU NEED THIS TO GO
old definition: A direct question that surfaces the executive's mandate and success criteria — asked when you want to understand what outcome they are personally accountable for delivering.
new definition: A question asking what result the other person wants to achieve.
old example: I can show you what the tool does. But before I do — where do you need this to go? What is the number you need to move, and by when? That will tell me which part of what we do is actually relevant to you.
new example: Before I show you anything, where do you need this to go?

old definition: A promise and a contract — signals that you understand the executive's time is scarce and that you have prepared accordingly. Only say this if you mean it and can deliver on it.
new definition: A phrase promising that you will keep what you say short.
old example: I will be brief. You gave me fifteen minutes and I have prepared for twelve. The headline is one number, one decision, and one reason to move now. After that, I want to hear from you.
new example: I will be brief, and I have prepared twelve minutes of the fifteen you gave me.

word: THE DECISION IN FRONT OF YOU IS
old definition: Distils a complex situation down to the single decision the executive actually needs to make — removes noise, focuses the conversation, and shows you have done the analytical work so they do not have to.
new definition: A phrase used to name the one choice the listener has to make.
old example: The decision in front of you is not whether to invest in pipeline tools — you have already decided that. The decision is whether to do it before your Q3 review or after. I want to make the case for before.
new example: The decision in front of you is whether to buy before or after your Q3 review.
