old definition: Something given up in order to move a negotiation forward. The rule in professional negotiation is that concessions must be traded, never given away — a concession without a return sets a precedent and signals that the original position was not serious.
new definition: Something you give up to help a negotiation move forward.
old example: Marcus asked for a 20% discount. Riley was willing to make a concession on price — but only if Marcus was willing to move on the contract length. A concession for nothing is not a negotiation; it is a reduction.
new example: We can make a small concession on delivery costs.

old definition: An exchange in which gaining something on one side requires giving up something on another. Trade-offs give both parties a way to move without losing face — because each side gets something, and each side gives something.
new definition: An exchange where gaining one thing means giving up another.
old example: Riley offered a trade-off: a lower unit price in exchange for a twelve-month commitment instead of six. Marcus got the number he needed for his budget. Riley got the contract length that made the reduction financially sensible.
new example: The trade-off is $299 a month for a much faster return.

old definition: To set the first number or term in a negotiation, establishing the reference point that all later discussion is measured against. Whoever anchors first controls the frame — which is why experienced negotiators anchor high before the other side can anchor first.
new definition: To set the first number or term, which becomes the reference point.
old example: Before Marcus could name a number, Riley anchored with the full annual contract value. When Marcus pushed back, the conversation was about how far to move from her number — not how far to move from his.
new example: She decided to anchor the discussion with our full annual price.

old definition: An earlier decision or action that becomes the standard or expectation for future situations. In price negotiation, giving a concession without conditions sets a precedent — the next time this prospect, or any prospect, opens a negotiation, they expect the same terms as a starting point.
new definition: An earlier action that becomes the expected standard for future situations.
old example: Riley was careful not to set a precedent with Marcus. A 20% discount with no conditions would mean every renewal conversation starting from that lower number. She structured the concession with conditions precisely to avoid this.
new example: A free upgrade now could set a precedent for every renewal.

old definition: The range of what is included in an agreement — how many users, how many features, how much support, how long the term. Adjusting scope is often a more sustainable negotiation move than adjusting price, because it changes what is being bought rather than what it costs.
new definition: The range of what an agreement includes, such as users, features, or support.
old example: When Marcus pushed on price, Riley shifted the conversation to scope. Could they start with a smaller team and expand in Q2? That gave Marcus a lower entry cost while preserving the unit price — and created a natural expansion conversation for later.
new example: Let's reduce the scope to one team and expand later.

old definition: The point beyond which a party cannot or will not go — a floor on price, a ceiling on concessions, or a boundary on terms. Understanding your own threshold before entering a negotiation is essential. Understanding the other side's threshold is what makes a deal possible.
new definition: The point beyond which someone will not go in a negotiation.
old example: Riley knew her threshold: below a certain unit price, the account was not profitable. She did not share that number, but she used it to structure every offer she made — nothing she proposed crossed her own floor, even when the conversation got uncomfortable.
new example: He explained that costs, delays and risks were now past our threshold.

old definition: Given or done in return for something equivalent. A reciprocal concession is one made in response to a move from the other side — it keeps both parties invested and signals that the negotiation is a two-way process, not a series of demands.
new definition: Given or done in return for something of equal value.
old example: Riley made a reciprocal concession: when Marcus agreed to a twelve-month commitment, she moved on implementation fees. The movement was in response to his movement — which made it feel earned rather than given, and kept both sides at the table.
new example: We would like a reciprocal concession if we lower the price.

old definition: The specific conditions and details of an agreement — payment schedule, contract length, support level, renewal clauses, and so on. Separating price from terms is a key negotiation move: often what looks like a price disagreement is actually a disagreement about terms.
new definition: The specific conditions and details of an agreement.
old example: Marcus said the price was too high. Riley asked him to separate the price from the terms: if the payment were spread across the year rather than billed upfront, would the monthly figure feel more manageable? It was the same total — but the terms changed the conversation.
new example: The price is fine, but I'd like to discuss the terms.

word: IF YOU CAN MOVE ON X, WE CAN MOVE ON Y
old definition: The structural language of conditional negotiation. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed — this phrase makes every concession explicitly conditional on a move from the other side.
new definition: A phrase that makes your concession depend on a move from the other side.
old example: 'If you can move to a twelve-month term, we can move on the unit price. I am not able to give you both — but I can give you one if you can give me the other.'
new example: If you can move on the contract length, we can move on price.

word: WHAT ARE YOU ABLE TO MOVE ON
old definition: A probe that tests the other side's flexibility without revealing your own floor. Forces the other party to identify where they have room before you show your hand.
new definition: A question that asks what flexibility the other side has.
old example: 'Before I respond to the pricing request, I want to understand the full picture. What are you able to move on from your side — contract length, payment terms, implementation timeline? That tells me where I have room to work.'
new example: Before I answer, what are you able to move on?

word: I CAN WORK WITH THAT — BUT ONLY IF
old definition: A conditional acceptance — signals that you are open to the other side's position, but makes your agreement explicitly dependent on a condition. Keeps flexibility visible without giving a free concession.
new definition: A phrase that accepts an idea, but only under a certain condition.
old example: 'I can work with a reduced entry price — but only if we structure the contract so that the rate steps back up at renewal unless the volume targets are hit. I need something to anchor the discount to.'
new example: I can work with that, but only if you commit to twelve months.

word: LET'S SEPARATE THE PRICE FROM THE TERMS
old definition: A reframe used when price negotiation is stuck. Moves the conversation to contract structure, payment schedule, scope, or other levers — often revealing that the real disagreement is about terms, not the total number.
new definition: A phrase that moves the talk from the total price to the agreement's structure.
old example: 'Let's separate the price from the terms for a moment. The annual figure is what it is — but if we talk about how it is structured, there may be more room than the headline number suggests. Monthly billing, phased implementation, a smaller initial scope?'
new example: Let's separate the price from the terms and look at billing.

word: THAT'S AT THE EDGE OF WHAT I CAN DO
old definition: Signals a threshold without making it personal, confrontational, or absolute. Keeps the door open while communicating that you are close to the limit — which invites the other side to move rather than simply saying no.
new definition: A phrase that says you are almost at your limit, politely.
old example: 'I want to find something that works for both of us — but what you are describing is at the edge of what I can do at this contract value. If we can bring in the volume commitment, I have a little more room. Without it, I am at the limit.'
new example: That's at the edge of what I can do on this order.

word: WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS WORK FOR YOU
old definition: An open probe that invites the other side to define what they actually need, rather than defending a position. Often reveals that what the prospect is asking for is different from what they actually need — and that there are creative solutions neither side has considered.
new definition: A question that asks the other side what they truly need.
old example: 'You've told me the price is a concern — I hear that. But before we talk numbers, help me understand: what would make this work for you? Is it the total cost, the cash flow timing, the risk of commitment, or something else? Because each of those has a different answer.'
new example: What would make this work for you?

old definition: A structured account that moves through a beginning, middle, and end. In sales, a narrative is more persuasive than presenting facts in isolation — because it gives the listener a way to locate themselves in the story and imagine the outcome for their own situation.
new definition: A story with a clear beginning, middle, and end that explains events.
old example: Riley did not list the product features. She built a narrative: a specific company, a real problem, a moment of change, and a measurable result. By the end, Marcus had not been sold to — he had been shown what was possible.
new example: She built a narrative around one client's problem and its solution.

old definition: The sense of risk, urgency, or unresolved conflict that makes a story worth hearing. Without tension, there is no reason for the listener to care about the outcome. Tension in a sales story comes from showing what was at stake if the problem was not solved.
new definition: A feeling of worry or pressure when the outcome is still uncertain.
old example: Riley did not rush past the problem. She held the tension: the team was losing two hours per rep per day, the quarter-end was approaching, and the VP of Sales was asking for answers. That pressure made the solution feel necessary, not optional.
new example: The tension in the room grew as the sales figures kept falling.

old definition: What was at risk if the problem remained unresolved — the cost of inaction in human, financial, or strategic terms. High stakes are what make tension feel real. A story without visible stakes is a description of a problem, not a story about one.
new definition: What you could lose or gain depending on how a situation turns out.
old example: The stakes in Riley's story were specific: the company was about to lose its third enterprise client in a row to a competitor with faster response times. That detail made the problem impossible to ignore — because Marcus recognised the same pressure in his own business.
new example: The stakes are high: we could lose revenue and our biggest customers.

old definition: The moment in a story where something changes — the decision, discovery, or intervention that shifts the trajectory from problem toward resolution. In a sales story, the turning point is usually when the solution enters, but it should feel like a story moment, not a product pitch.
new definition: The moment in a story when things begin to change.
old example: Riley described the turning point not as 'they implemented our software' but as 'the week their ops lead stopped spending Fridays building manual reports and started spending them coaching the team.' That shift — from describing a feature to naming a moment — made Marcus lean forward.
new example: The turning point came when the team finally saw the new strategy.

old definition: The point in a story where the tension is released and the outcome becomes clear. A strong resolution is specific and measurable — it shows what changed in terms the listener can evaluate. A vague resolution ('things got better') is almost as ineffective as having no resolution at all.
new definition: The part of a story where the problem is solved and the result is clear.
old example: Riley's resolution was precise: twelve weeks after implementation, the team's average response time dropped from four hours to forty minutes, and the client retention rate recovered by 18 percentage points. The resolution gave Marcus something concrete to take to his CFO.
new example: The resolution was simple: both sides shook hands and signed the deal.

old definition: The central character in a story — in sales, usually a customer or user whose experience the prospect can identify with. For a sales story to land, the prospect must be able to see themselves in the protagonist. A protagonist who is too different from your audience makes the story feel irrelevant.
new definition: The main character in a story.
old example: Riley chose her protagonist carefully: a VP of Sales at a B2B software company with 25 reps, a fast-growth mandate, and a workflow problem that was invisible to the C-suite. Marcus had 22 reps. The similarity was not an accident.
new example: In my story, the protagonist is a director who is facing a difficult decision.

old definition: Producing strong, clear mental images through specific details — names, numbers, moments, and sensory descriptions — rather than generalisations. Vivid storytelling makes abstract value concrete. The more specific a detail, the more real the story feels, even to someone who was not there.
new definition: Described with clear, specific details that create strong pictures in your mind.
old example: Riley did not say 'the team was overwhelmed.' She said 'by Thursday afternoon, the support queue had 340 open tickets and the team lead had stopped answering Slack messages.' The specific number and the specific behaviour made the scene visible — which made it believable.
new example: Her description of the overdue invoices and the empty warehouse was vivid.

old definition: The quality of connecting deeply with someone's own experience — the feeling that a story is describing something the listener recognises, not just something that happened to someone else. A story has resonance when the prospect says — out loud or internally — 'that is exactly what is happening to us.'
new definition: The quality of feeling familiar and meaningful to someone because it matches their experience.
old example: Halfway through Riley's story, Marcus stopped taking notes. He was no longer evaluating the story — he was inside it. That moment of resonance — where the protagonist's situation became his situation — was worth more than any slide in the deck.
new example: My story clearly had resonance with you, since you know that feeling too.

word: LET ME TELL YOU ABOUT A CUSTOMER WHO
old definition: The opening line that signals a story is coming. It shifts the register from pitch to conversation, invites the prospect to listen rather than evaluate, and positions what follows as evidence rather than assertion.
new definition: A phrase used to begin a short story about a real customer.
old example: 'Let me tell you about a customer who had almost exactly the situation you are describing — because I think the way it resolved is relevant to the conversation we are having today.'
new example: Let me tell you about a customer who struggled with exactly this issue.

old definition: The line that sets up the problem clearly and specifically — not as a category ('they had an efficiency issue') but as a concrete, named situation. The more specific the problem, the more the prospect recognises it.
new definition: A phrase used to introduce the main difficulty in a story.
old example: 'The problem was that every time a new enterprise client onboarded, the same three people had to drop everything for two weeks. It was not a capacity problem — it was a process problem that looked like a capacity problem, and no one had separated the two.'
new example: The problem was that every new client created two weeks of extra work.

old definition: The tension escalator — a second detail that deepens the urgency of the problem before the solution arrives. Used to hold the tension longer, which makes the turning point feel more earned when it comes.
new definition: A phrase used to add another difficulty that makes a situation more serious.
old example: 'What made it worse was that the board had just approved headcount for three new enterprise sales reps — which meant the onboarding problem was about to get significantly larger before anyone had fixed it.'
new example: What made it worse was that three new reps were about to start.

old definition: The phrase that introduces the solution or intervention — but as a story moment, not a product feature. The turning point should describe a change in what someone was able to do, not a change in what software they were using.
new definition: A phrase used to introduce the moment when a situation began to improve.
old example: 'The turning point was when the ops lead ran the first automated onboarding sequence and realised she had been doing manually in two weeks what the system did in four hours. That was the moment the conversation with leadership changed.'
new example: The turning point was when we saw the whole process run in four hours.

old definition: A time marker that creates narrative distance between the problem and the outcome, making the resolution feel earned rather than immediate. Can be adapted — 'six weeks later', 'by the end of Q3' — but always puts the outcome at a credible remove from the intervention.
new definition: A phrase that moves a story forward in time to show the result.
old example: 'Three months later, the average onboarding time had dropped from fourteen days to three. The three new sales reps the board had approved were fully supported. And the ops lead was spending her Fridays on process improvement instead of manual configuration.'
new example: Three months later, onboarding took three days instead of fourteen.

word: WHAT THAT MEANT FOR THEM WAS
old definition: The translation layer — converts the outcome from a metric into a business impact the prospect can evaluate. Not 'the product worked' but 'what that meant in practice was that they stopped losing enterprise clients to a competitor with a faster response time.'
new definition: A phrase used to explain the real effect or benefit of a result.
old example: 'What that meant for them was that they closed Q4 as their best quarter in three years — not because the market changed, but because the team finally had the headroom to do the work they had been hired to do.'
new example: What that meant for them was their strongest quarter in years.

old definition: The quality of requiring prompt attention or action. In sales, genuine urgency is rooted in the prospect's situation — what changes, costs more, or becomes harder the longer the decision is delayed. The difference between real urgency and manufactured pressure is whether the consequence of waiting belongs to the prospect or to the seller.
new definition: The feeling that something needs attention or action very soon.
old example: Riley did not create urgency by inventing a deadline. She created it by making the cost of waiting specific: every month Marcus delayed, three more reps were operating on a broken process, and the gap between his team and his competitor's was compounding. The urgency was already in his numbers — she just made it visible.
new example: The urgency comes from your own numbers, not from any deadline of mine.

old definition: The state of not making a decision or taking a step forward. In B2B sales, inaction is rarely neutral — it carries a cost that accumulates over time. Making the cost of inaction specific and visible is what separates genuine urgency from pressure tactics.
new definition: The failure to act or make a decision.
old example: Marcus had not decided to stay with the status quo — he had simply not decided to change it. Riley's job was to help him see that inaction was itself a decision, and that decision had a price: twelve months of compounding inefficiency, a competitor gaining ground, and an ops lead whose frustration was approaching the point of departure.
new example: Inaction is already costing your team forty hours of manual work every week.

old definition: The energy and direction a conversation, project, or decision process carries. Momentum is fragile — delays kill it, and restarting a stalled conversation requires significantly more effort than continuing one that is already moving. In sales, one of the real costs of 'let's revisit in Q1' is the loss of everything both sides built toward the decision.
new definition: The forward energy that keeps a process or decision moving.
old example: Riley and Marcus had spent three meetings reaching the point where the case was clear and the internal support was there. A deferral to Q1 would not pause that progress — it would reset it. New quarter, new priorities, new reasons to delay. Riley named the cost of losing momentum before Marcus had a chance to treat it as a free option.
new example: We have built real momentum over the last three meetings.

old definition: To increase or accumulate over time at an accelerating rate — making something larger, worse, or more expensive the longer it is left unaddressed. Problems that compound are more urgent than problems that stay constant, because the cost of waiting grows rather than holding steady.
new definition: To grow worse or larger over time as effects build on each other.
old example: Every quarter Marcus delayed, the efficiency gap between his team and the competitor who had started in January compounded. The first month of delay cost him one month of results. The third month of delay cost him three months of compounding advantage — the numbers were not linear.
new example: Those onboarding delays will compound with every new rep you hire.

old definition: The act of postponing a decision or action to a later point. A deferral is not the same as a rejection — but it is not cost-free either. Naming the specific cost of a deferral is the key move in creating urgency without pressure: not 'you must decide now' but 'here is what changes if you decide in February instead of today.'
new definition: The act of delaying a decision until a later time.
old example: Marcus's default was deferral — not because he did not see the value, but because a decision required effort and the status quo required none. Riley did not argue against the deferral. She priced it: three months of deferral at two hours per rep per day, across twenty-two reps, was roughly four hundred hours of selling time lost to a problem she could fix in six weeks.
new example: A deferral until February would add three more months of manual reporting.

old definition: An event or condition that triggers or accelerates a change. In sales, tying urgency to a real external catalyst — a competitor move, a budget cycle reset, a regulatory deadline, a leadership change — makes it credible and prospect-owned rather than seller-manufactured. The best catalysts are things the prospect already knows about.
new definition: Something that causes a change or makes it happen faster.
old example: The catalyst Riley used was Marcus's own Q3 review: his CEO had flagged sales process efficiency as a strategic priority for the year, and Q1 budgets were being set in six weeks. Riley did not invent the catalyst — she named the one that already existed and connected it to the decision on the table.
new example: Your CEO's new efficiency target is the catalyst for this decision.

old definition: To gradually diminish or wear away over time — often without a visible moment of loss. Competitive advantages erode. Market positions erode. The internal support for a decision can erode if a project stalls long enough for stakeholders to lose interest or shift priorities. Things that erode are more urgent than things that simply wait.
new definition: To slowly wear away or become weaker over time.
old example: Riley warned Marcus about something that did not feel like a crisis but was: the goodwill she had built with his CFO over three conversations would erode if the project went quiet for a quarter. By the time the conversation restarted, the relationship would need rebuilding and the case would need re-presenting. That was not a hypothetical — it was a pattern she had seen before.
new example: Internal support for the project will erode if it stays quiet for a quarter.

old definition: Acting in anticipation of a future problem or opportunity rather than reacting after the fact. The language of urgency without pressure is fundamentally proactive — it helps the prospect act before the cost is undeniable rather than after it has already been paid.
new definition: Acting early to deal with a problem before it happens.
old example: Riley reframed the decision as proactive rather than reactive. Marcus did not have a crisis — yet. But the companies that were six months ahead of him had once been in the same position. They had made a proactive decision before the problem became urgent enough to be obvious. That was the choice on the table.
new example: Starting now is a proactive step, not a reaction to a crisis.

old definition: The core urgency phrase — names the specific cost of inaction without inventing a deadline or applying pressure. What follows must be concrete, prospect-specific, and true. Generic versions ('you'll fall behind competitors') have no effect. Specific versions ('your competitor who started this in January will have six months of compounding advantage by Q2') create genuine urgency.
new definition: A phrase used to name the specific cost of delaying a decision.
old example: 'The risk of waiting until Q1 is not that the product will be unavailable — it is that your competitor who started this in January will have six months of embedded process and compounding efficiency gains before your team starts day one. That gap is not impossible to close. But it grows every month.'
new example: The risk of waiting is that your team spends another quarter on manual reporting.

old definition: A compounding frame that makes the cost of delay accumulate visibly. Works by translating the abstract cost of inaction into a running total the prospect can calculate. Most effective when followed by a specific number — hours, dollars, clients, or percentage points.
new definition: A phrase that shows the cost of delay growing with each passing month.
old example: 'Every month this is unresolved, your team is spending roughly forty hours per rep on manual processes that this system handles automatically. That is 880 hours across the team — per month. By Q1, you will have spent the equivalent of five full-time months of selling time on something that is already fixed for your competitor.'
new example: Every month this is unresolved, your reps lose roughly forty hours each.

word: WHAT CHANGES IF YOU WAIT UNTIL
old definition: A question that forces the prospect to evaluate the deferral explicitly — to name what they think will be different in Q1 or after the next board meeting. Often reveals that the prospect has not actually thought through what changes, and that the conditions for the decision are already present.
new definition: A question asking what will be different after the prospect delays the decision.
old example: 'What changes if you wait until February? I want to understand what you are waiting for — because if the answer is that the budget opens, we can work around that now. If the answer is that the team will have more capacity, I want to check that assumption against what Q1 actually looks like for your ops team.'
new example: What changes if you wait until February to sign the agreement?

old definition: A market-reality frame that positions the prospect relative to what others in their space are already doing. Effective only when true and specific — 'two of the companies in your sector started this in Q3' is credible; 'everyone is doing this' is not.
new definition: A phrase saying a rival company began the same project at a certain time.
old example: 'I can tell you that two of the companies in your sector — one of which you have mentioned as a benchmark — started this in Q3. They are now three months into what takes most teams six to eight months to fully embed. By the time you start in Q1, they will have a quarter-head start that is very difficult to close quickly.'
new example: Your competitor started this in March and is already seeing faster onboarding.

word: BY THE TIME YOU ARE READY TO ACT
old definition: A forward-looking consequence frame — paints a specific picture of what the landscape looks like if the decision is delayed until the prospect feels completely comfortable. Used to make the future cost visible without threatening or pressuring.
new definition: A phrase describing how the situation will look after a long delay.
old example: 'By the time you are ready to act in Q2, the onboarding backlog that is currently three accounts will be six. Your two new reps will have spent a full quarter in a process that is already broken. And the internal case you would need to make to your CFO will be harder — not because the product changed, but because the urgency will feel less fresh.'
new example: By the time you are ready to act, the backlog will have doubled.

word: I AM NOT TRYING TO RUSH YOU — BUT
old definition: A frame that explicitly separates the salesperson's position from pressure tactics, then names a genuine cost of waiting. The phrase works by acknowledging that the prospect has the right to move at their own pace, while making the cost of that pace visible. The 'but' must be followed by something specific — not a vague warning.
new definition: A phrase that softens what follows by saying you are not applying pressure.
old example: 'I am not trying to rush you — but I want to make sure the decision is made with full information about what waiting costs. The risk of getting to Q2 and starting from zero is not a sales concern — it is a business one. And I would rather name it now than have you discover it in April.'
new example: I am not trying to rush you, but the onboarding backlog is growing weekly.

old definition: To reduce the intensity of a conflict or emotional situation — bringing the temperature down so that productive conversation can happen. De-escalation always comes before problem-solving: a customer who feels unheard cannot be helped, and attempting to explain or solve before they feel acknowledged will intensify the conflict, not reduce it.
new definition: To reduce the tension or anger in a conflict or emotional situation.
old example: Marcus was furious when he called — his voice was raised, his language was sharp, and he had a list of failures he intended to work through. Riley did not interrupt him. She let him finish, then de-escalated before she said a single word about what had happened: 'I can hear how frustrated you are, and I want to make sure I understand everything before I respond.'
new example: I'll try to de-escalate this before both clients walk out.

old definition: The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person — and, in professional contexts, to express that understanding in a way the other person can hear. In customer service, expressed empathy is the difference between a customer who calms down and one who intensifies. It must be genuine and specific — scripted empathy is usually worse than none at all.
new definition: The ability to understand and share another person's feelings.
old example: Riley did not say 'I understand your frustration' — which Marcus would have heard as a formula. She said 'I can imagine what it felt like to discover this on a Monday morning with your team waiting on you.' The specificity was what made the empathy land. She had listened well enough to use his detail, not a template.
new example: Her empathy for the upset customer helped calm the whole call.

old definition: Calm, controlled self-presentation in a stressful or confrontational situation. Maintaining composure is a professional skill — it can be practised, and it has specific language patterns that help. The most important thing composure signals to a difficult customer is that the person on the other side of the conversation is not going to match their intensity — which often reduces the intensity itself.
new definition: A calm, controlled manner, especially in a stressful situation.
old example: When Marcus raised his voice, Riley lowered hers. When he repeated himself, she slowed down. When he said something unkind, she paused before responding. None of these were passive — they were deliberate composure techniques that changed the emotional dynamic of the conversation without a single word about how he was speaking to her.
new example: She kept her composure even when the customer started shouting.

old definition: To explicitly confirm that something happened, that it matters, and that the person affected deserved better. Acknowledging a problem is not the same as accepting full responsibility or agreeing with every aspect of the customer's account — but it is the step that must come before any explanation, justification, or solution. Skipping acknowledgement makes everything that follows sound like a defence.
new definition: To openly recognise that something happened and that it mattered.
old example: Riley acknowledged the failure before she explained anything: 'What you experienced on Thursday was not acceptable, and your team should not have been in that position.' Only after that did she explain what had happened — and by then, Marcus was ready to hear it rather than argue against it.
new example: I acknowledge that the delivery delay caused you real inconvenience.

old definition: To reduce the tension or danger in a difficult situation by removing or addressing the element that is driving the intensity. In customer conversations, defusing anger usually requires addressing the emotion first and the practical problem second — in that order. Reversing the order — jumping to solutions while the customer is still emotionally activated — almost never works.
new definition: To make a tense or angry situation calmer.
old example: Riley defused the call in three moves: she let Marcus finish speaking without interruption, she acknowledged the impact of the failure in his own terms, and she asked one question about how his team had been affected. By the time she moved to what had caused the problem, the anger had reduced to frustration — which is a conversation she could have.
new example: A sincere apology helped him defuse the complaint quickly.

old definition: Handling sensitive or difficult conversations in a way that achieves honesty without unnecessary confrontation. Diplomatic language is precise, not evasive — it says the difficult thing in a way the other person can hear. The opposite of diplomatic is not honest — it is blunt without care for how the message lands.
new definition: Careful and tactful when dealing with sensitive or difficult subjects.
old example: Riley needed to tell Marcus that part of the failure had been caused by his team's configuration choices. She did not say 'your team made an error.' She said: 'Part of what contributed to this was a configuration decision made at setup — and I want to walk through that together so we can prevent it from happening again.' The content was the same. The delivery made it possible to hear.
new example: He gave a diplomatic answer when the client criticised the price.

old definition: The quality or character of speech — in how words are delivered — that expresses attitude, emotion, or intent. In customer service, tone is often more important than content: the same words delivered with impatience, condescension, or defensiveness produce a completely different outcome than the same words delivered with calm, warmth, and focus. Tone is what the customer feels after a conversation, even when they cannot quote exactly what was said.
new definition: The attitude or feeling that comes through in the way someone speaks.
old example: After the call, Marcus told his colleague: 'She was straight with me about what happened, but somehow I felt better rather than worse.' He could not explain why. The reason was tone: Riley had delivered difficult information — including information that reflected badly on his own team — in a tone that was consistently warm, direct, and focused on resolution. The content had not changed. The tone had made it receivable.
new example: The customer was upset by the tone of my reply.

old definition: A professional limit on what is acceptable in a working relationship. In difficult customer situations, clear and calm boundary-setting is sometimes necessary — and doing it without confrontation or defensiveness is a key professional skill. A boundary is not a threat; it is a statement about what kind of conversation can be productive.
new definition: A limit on what behaviour you will accept from another person.
old example: When Marcus's language became personal, Riley set a boundary without raising her voice: 'I want to resolve this for you — and I can do that best if we keep the conversation focused on what happened and what we do next. Can we do that?' She did not tell him what he was doing wrong. She told him what she needed in order to help him. The distinction made it possible for him to hear it.
new example: I had to set a boundary when the customer began shouting.

word: I CAN HEAR THAT THIS HAS BEEN FRUSTRATING
old definition: An empathy opener that names the customer's emotion specifically — not a generic 'I understand' but a statement that reflects back what they are actually feeling. 'I can hear' signals that you have been listening, not just waiting to respond. Using the word 'frustrating' validates the emotion without amplifying it.
new definition: A phrase that names the customer's annoyance and shows you are listening.
old example: 'I can hear that this has been an incredibly frustrating experience — especially given that you had prepared your team for the launch and this disrupted everything they were depending on. That is not what should have happened, and I want to make sure we fix it.'
new example: I can hear that this has been frustrating for you.

word: LET ME MAKE SURE I UNDERSTAND WHAT HAPPENED
old definition: A de-escalation probe that slows the conversation, signals full engagement, and gives the customer a structured opportunity to feel heard before you respond. By asking to understand rather than jumping to explain, you signal that their account of events is being taken seriously — which reduces defensiveness on both sides.
new definition: A phrase used to slow down and check the facts before responding.
old example: 'Before I respond, let me make sure I understand what happened — because I want to get this right, not give you a general answer. Walk me through Thursday from your side. What did your team see first?'
new example: Let me make sure I understand what happened on Thursday.

word: THAT IS NOT THE EXPERIENCE WE WANT YOU TO HAVE
old definition: An acknowledgement phrase that confirms the failure without excessive self-blame or defensive explanation. It connects the customer's experience to the standard they should expect — which validates their right to be unhappy without over-apologising in a way that can feel hollow or create liability.
new definition: A phrase that admits a failure and says it falls below your standards.
old example: 'What you described on Thursday — the system going down at 9am with no prior warning and no response for two hours — that is not the experience we want you to have. You are right to be frustrated, and I am not going to minimise that.'
new example: A three-week delay is not the experience we want you to have.

old definition: A diplomatic redirect that names what is possible rather than leading with what is not. 'What I can do is' keeps the conversation solution-focused and avoids the dead-end energy of 'I can't do that' or 'that's not our policy.' It also signals agency — the person you are speaking to is telling you what they are able to offer, not hiding behind a rule.
new definition: A phrase that introduces the options that are actually available.
old example: 'I understand you want a full refund for the month — and I want to be transparent with you about what I can approve directly. What I can do is credit you for the downtime period and escalate the refund question to our account director today. I will have an answer for you before the end of the day.'
new example: What I can do is arrange a replacement by Friday.

word: I WANT TO BE TRANSPARENT WITH YOU
old definition: A composure phrase that signals honest, direct communication is coming — often used when the news is difficult or when part of the failure involves something the customer may not want to hear. It pre-frames the next sentence as honest rather than evasive, which means the customer is more likely to receive it without resistance.
new definition: A phrase that signals you are about to speak openly and honestly.
old example: 'I want to be transparent with you about what we found when we investigated Thursday. Part of what contributed to the downtime was a configuration setting that was changed during your team's onboarding. I am not saying this to deflect — I am saying it because understanding the cause is the only way to prevent it from happening again.'
new example: I want to be transparent with you about the cause of the delay.

word: LET'S FOCUS ON WHAT WE CAN RESOLVE RIGHT NOW
old definition: A de-escalation close that moves the conversation from grievance to action — useful when a customer is circling the same complaint repeatedly or when the conversation has been productive but needs to move toward resolution. It acknowledges that there is more to discuss without letting the grievance phase continue indefinitely.
new definition: A phrase that moves a conversation from complaints toward practical solutions.
old example: 'I hear everything you are saying — and there is more to discuss about the root cause and the process changes we need to make. But I want to make sure we do not end this call without resolving the immediate impact on your team. Let's focus on what we can fix right now, and then I will schedule a follow-up for the broader conversation.'
new example: Let's focus on what we can resolve right now, starting with the invoice.

old definition: Anyone with an interest in or influence over a purchasing decision. In complex B2B sales, a deal typically involves multiple stakeholders — users, managers, executives, and buyers — each with different priorities and different definitions of success. Failing to identify all of them is one of the most common reasons deals stall after a strong initial conversation.
new definition: A person with an interest in a decision or some influence over it.
old example: Riley had been speaking exclusively to Marcus for three meetings — and only in the fourth meeting did she discover that the CFO, the Head of IT, and two senior users were all stakeholders in the decision. Each of them needed a different version of the conversation she had been having with Marcus alone.
new example: The CFO is a key stakeholder in this purchase.

old definition: A defined profile representing a type of decision-maker — based on their role, their priorities, what success looks like for them, and what they are most afraid of. Different personas require different language, different metrics, and different emotional appeals, even when the product being described is identical.
new definition: A profile describing a type of decision-maker, including their role and priorities.
old example: Riley built a one-page persona map before the multi-stakeholder meeting: the CFO persona was focused on ROI and risk; the Head of IT persona was focused on integration and security; the senior users persona was focused on learning curve and whether the tool would actually save them time. Same meeting, three fundamentally different conversations.
new example: We wrote a separate persona for the finance director.

old definition: A person inside the prospect's organisation who advocates for your solution internally — attending meetings you are not in, answering questions you cannot hear, and building the internal case on your behalf. Identifying and equipping a champion is often more important than the quality of the external pitch, because the internal conversation is the one that actually determines most decisions.
new definition: An internal supporter who promotes your product inside the client's company.
old example: Marcus had become Riley's champion without either of them using the word. He was forwarding her emails to the CFO, repeating her arguments in meetings she was not invited to, and flagging the competitor threat in his weekly report. Riley's job was to give him the language, the data, and the story he needed to do that effectively.
new example: The IT manager became our champion during the internal review.

old definition: Return on Investment — the financial return generated by a decision relative to its cost. Executive and buyer audiences require a credible ROI conversation before approving a significant purchase. The ROI must be specific, defensible, and expressed in terms the audience already uses to measure success — not in terms the vendor has invented.
new definition: Return on investment: the financial gain from a purchase compared with its cost.
old example: When Riley met the CFO, she did not talk about features or workflow improvements. She talked about ROI: the average time-to-value for accounts of similar size was eleven weeks, the efficiency gain translated to approximately 880 freed hours per month across the team, and the cost of the contract was recovered — at conservative assumptions — within one quarter. The CFO asked two follow-up questions. That was when Riley knew the number was right.
new example: The CFO wanted to see the projected ROI before approving.

old definition: The process by which a new tool, system, or process becomes genuinely embedded in an organisation's daily workflow — not just purchased, but actually used. Manager and user audiences care about adoption more than executives, because they are the ones who have to make it happen. A solution that is bought but not adopted is, from the organisation's perspective, a failed investment.
new definition: The point when people begin using a new tool regularly in their work.
old example: The Head of Sales had approved three tools in the past two years that had never reached full adoption — bought by the executive team, resisted by the users, and eventually abandoned. When Riley spoke to the team leads, she spent more time on the onboarding experience and the support structure than on the ROI. Adoption was the conversation they needed to have before the one about results.
new example: The team leads were worried about adoption after the rollout.

old definition: The capacity to affect a decision or outcome without having formal authority over it. In complex B2B sales, influence often matters as much as authority — the senior user who tells the VP the team will never use this can kill a deal the CFO has already approved. Mapping influence, not just hierarchy, is what separates experienced from inexperienced salespeople.
new definition: The power to affect a decision without having official authority over it.
old example: The Head of IT had no formal authority over the purchasing decision — but his opinion on security and integration carried significant weight with the CTO, who did. Riley spent forty-five minutes with the Head of IT on a call that no one told her she needed to have. Three days later, the concern about data compliance disappeared from the conversation.
new example: The senior user has real influence over the final decision.

old definition: Agreement reached across multiple people or perspectives. In complex B2B sales, decisions often require consensus among stakeholders who have different, sometimes competing, priorities. The salesperson's job is not just to convince each individual — it is to understand how those individuals will reach agreement with each other, and to make that process easier.
new definition: General agreement among a group of people.
old example: The deal was stalling because the CFO and the Head of Operations had different views on the implementation timeline. Neither was wrong — they just had different constraints. Riley did not try to convince one of them to change their position. She proposed a phased implementation that gave the CFO the financial structure she needed and gave Operations the preparation time they required. Consensus was not a compromise — it was a redesign.
new example: The committee has not yet reached a consensus on the timeline.

old definition: The specific statement of value or benefit being offered to a particular audience. In a multi-stakeholder sale, the proposition must be adapted for each decision-maker — the same features become different benefits depending on who is listening. A proposition that works perfectly for a VP of Sales will usually fail completely with a CFO, even when the underlying product is identical.
new definition: The specific value or benefit you offer to a particular audience.
old example: Riley prepared four versions of her proposition for the multi-stakeholder meeting. For the users: you will spend less time on the parts of your job that are not actually your job. For the manager: your team will onboard new clients in three days instead of fourteen. For the CFO: the investment is recovered within one quarter at conservative assumptions. For procurement: the contract includes a service level agreement with financial penalties for downtime above 0.1%.
new example: Our proposition is simple: an integrated platform that increases your direct bookings.

word: WHAT DOES SUCCESS LOOK LIKE FOR YOU
old definition: The universal opening probe for any new stakeholder — surfaces what they actually care about before you assume it from their job title. A CFO and a VP of Sales in the same company may define success in completely different terms, and getting this wrong means delivering the right answer to the wrong question.
new definition: A question asking what result the person personally wants to achieve.
old example: Before I walk you through how this works, I want to make sure I understand what success looks like for you specifically — because the Head of Sales and the CFO have described it quite differently, and I want to make sure this conversation is useful for your role rather than a repeat of one you have already had.
new example: What does success look like for you in the first year?

word: IN YOUR ROLE, WHAT MATTERS MOST IS
old definition: A persona-specific framing device — signals that you have adapted your message to the person in front of you rather than delivering a standard pitch. It also invites correction: if your assumption about what matters to them is wrong, they will tell you before you have spent twenty minutes on the wrong thing.
new definition: A phrase that introduces the priority you believe is most important in their job.
old example: In your role as Head of Operations, what matters most is probably whether your team can actually adopt this without disrupting the quarter — not whether the ROI model holds up on paper. So I want to start there, rather than with the number I showed the CFO.
new example: In your role, what matters most is keeping downtime close to zero.

word: THE WAY YOUR TEAM WOULD FEEL THIS IS
old definition: The translation phrase for user and manager conversations — converts features and business metrics into day-to-day experience. Users do not think in ROI; they think in time, frustration, and workflow. The way your team would feel this puts the value in terms they can evaluate from their own experience.
new definition: A phrase that describes a benefit as the team's daily experience.
old example: The way your team would feel this in the first month is: the Friday afternoon report that currently takes three hours gets done automatically overnight. That is not an efficiency gain on a slide — that is three hours back, every week, for every person on the team.
new example: The way your team would feel this is fewer manual reports every Friday.

old definition: The pivot phrase for executive conversations — signals that what follows is about strategic impact, competitive position, or financial return, not product features or day-to-day workflow. Executives do not buy tools; they buy outcomes. From a business perspective is the signal that you are about to speak their language.
new definition: A phrase that introduces a point about company strategy, money, or results.
old example: From a business perspective, the question is not whether the tool saves time — it does. The question is whether that time translates into measurable revenue impact. At similar companies, the freed capacity has been redirected to pipeline activity, and the average result is a 12% increase in deals advanced per rep per quarter.
new example: From a business perspective, this pays for itself within one quarter.

word: WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR BUDGET IS
old definition: The buyer and procurement frame — translates value into the financial and risk terms that purchasing and finance audiences need to evaluate. Procurement does not care that the sales team will be more productive; they care about total cost of ownership, contract risk, vendor stability, and whether the investment is defensible.
new definition: A phrase that introduces the financial effect of an offer.
old example: What this means for your budget is a fixed annual cost with no variable charges, a service level agreement with financial penalties for any downtime above 0.1%, and a standard data processing agreement that your legal team can approve without custom negotiation. I want to make the procurement process as straightforward as possible.
new example: What this means for your budget is one fixed annual fee.

word: WHO ELSE NEEDS TO SEE THIS
old definition: A stakeholder-mapping probe — surfaces other decision-makers or influencers without making the current person feel their authority is being questioned. Phrased as a process question rather than a challenge, it positions you as someone trying to help the deal succeed rather than someone trying to go around the person in front of you.
new definition: A question asking which other people should be involved in the decision.
old example: Before we move to next steps — who else needs to see this, or be part of the conversation? I want to make sure the right people have what they need, and I would rather map that now than discover a missing conversation three weeks from now when we are trying to close.
new example: Who else needs to see this before we finalise the contract?

old definition: A question that goes deeper than the first answer to find out what is really happening. Probing helps you get past surface-level information.
new definition: A question that digs deeper than the first answer to find the real cause.
old example: Good probing goes beneath the surface answer to find what's actually driving the decision.
new example: Her probing questions moved the conversation from the surface issue to the real reason behind the delay.

old definition: A question you ask to make sure you understand exactly what someone means. It turns a vague answer into something clear and specific.
new definition: A question that checks you have understood exactly what someone means.
old example: When a client says they want something 'better', a clarifying question turns that vague word into something you can actually respond to.
new example: He asked a clarifying question to find out which car size she actually had in mind.

old definition: Something you believe is true without checking. In sales, acting on untested assumptions can lead you to solve the wrong problem.
new definition: Something you believe is true without having checked it.
old example: The most dangerous assumptions are the ones no one in the room has thought to question yet.
new example: We built the whole plan on an assumption about sweater demand that nobody had tested.

old definition: To look at a problem from a different angle. A good reframe helps the buyer see their situation in a new way without telling them they are wrong.
new definition: To present a problem in a new way so people see it differently.
old example: A well-timed reframe doesn't tell the buyer they're wrong — it offers a new angle that makes a different conclusion feel obvious.
new example: Let me reframe the drop in sales as a chance to reach a new market.

old definition: The result of a problem if nothing changes. Showing the buyer the implication of staying the same makes the cost of not acting real and urgent.
new definition: A likely result or consequence that follows from a situation or decision.
old example: Spelling out the implication of a problem — what it costs the business month by month — turns a vague concern into something urgent.
new example: The main implication of these delays is that our biggest clients may lose trust in us.

old definition: An idea you think might be true, but have not confirmed yet. You share it with the buyer and ask them to agree or correct you.
new definition: An idea that might be true but has not yet been confirmed.
old example: Starting with a hypothesis gives the conversation direction while still leaving room to be corrected.
new example: My hypothesis is that the new campaign will lift sales, but we need to test it.

old definition: A questioning style that helps the other person find the answer themselves, instead of being told what to think. The goal is to guide, not to tell.
new definition: Describing a way of asking questions that helps people reach answers on their own.
old example: The Socratic approach works best when you want the buyer to reach the conclusion through their own reasoning rather than being told.
new example: Her Socratic style meant she never gave answers, only questions that made me think.

old definition: A questioning structure that starts broad and gets more specific. You begin with open questions and slowly narrow down to the key issue.
new definition: A method of questioning that begins with broad questions and narrows to specific ones.
old example: Start broad with open questions, then use the funnel technique to narrow toward the specific issue you want to understand.
new example: I used a funnel approach, starting with your goals and ending with the one issue slowing you down.

word: CAN YOU HELP ME UNDERSTAND WHAT YOU MEAN BY...?
old definition: A polite phrase used to ask someone to explain what they said more clearly. It is more respectful than asking 'What do you mean?'
new definition: A polite request for someone to explain their words more clearly.
old example: Can you help me understand what you mean by 'better value' — are you thinking about price, terms, or the overall package?
new example: Can you help me understand what you mean by a more classic piece?

word: WHAT'S BEHIND THAT — WHAT LED YOU TO THAT VIEW?
old definition: A phrase used to ask why someone thinks or feels a certain way. It helps you find the real reason behind their position.
new definition: A polite question asking why someone holds a particular opinion.
old example: What's behind that concern — is it something that came up in your last internal review, or feedback from someone on the team?
new example: What's behind that view, and what led you to think the supplier is the problem?

word: I'D LIKE TO CHALLENGE THAT ASSUMPTION GENTLY — HAVE YOU CONSIDERED...?
old definition: A polite way to question something the buyer believes without making them feel wrong. It opens up a new way of thinking.
new definition: A gentle way to question someone's belief and suggest another possibility.
old example: I'd like to challenge that assumption gently — the evidence we're seeing actually points in a different direction.
new example: I'd like to challenge that assumption gently: have you considered that the board may prefer the other approach?

word: IF THAT'S THE CASE, WHAT DOES THAT MEAN FOR...?
old definition: A phrase used to ask the buyer what happens next if the problem stays the same. It makes the cost of not acting feel real.
new definition: A question asking what the result will be if a situation stays the same.
old example: If that pattern continues for another six months, what does that mean for your team's end-of-year target?
new example: If that's the case, what does that mean for your team's workload and your service ratings?

word: WHAT WOULD SUCCESS LOOK LIKE FROM YOUR PERSPECTIVE?
old definition: A question that asks the buyer to describe what a good result looks like for them. It shifts the conversation from problems to outcomes.
new definition: A question asking someone to describe the result they would be happy with.
old example: Before I put anything forward, what would success look like from your perspective — how would you know in twelve months that this had worked?
new example: Before we talk about the proposal, what would success look like from your perspective?

word: IS THAT A FIXED CONSTRAINT, OR IS THERE SOME FLEXIBILITY THERE?
old definition: A question that checks whether a limit the buyer mentioned is real or can be changed. Many constraints in sales are flexible.
new definition: A question asking whether a limit is truly unchangeable or could be adjusted.
old example: Is that a fixed constraint, or is there some flexibility there if the right conditions were in place?
new example: Is that a fixed constraint, or is there some flexibility there on the budget?

old definition: The feeling a message gives the listener — warm, formal, direct, or careful. In cross-cultural sales, tone matters as much as the words you use.
new definition: The attitude or feeling that your voice and words give to the listener.
old example: The same message delivered in a warmer, slower tone can feel completely different from the same words said quickly and directly.
new example: Her calm, friendly tone made the client feel comfortable about the price.

old definition: How clearly and openly a person says what they mean. Some cultures value high directness; others prefer a softer, more indirect approach. Knowing the difference helps you adapt.
new definition: How openly and clearly a person says exactly what they mean.
old example: Adjusting your level of directness to match the other person's communication style shows cultural awareness and builds trust faster.
new example: His directness surprised the buyer, who preferred a softer way of negotiating.

old definition: Language tools used to keep a conversation respectful and comfortable. Examples include softening a request, hedging a disagreement, or giving a compliment before raising a concern.
new definition: Ways of speaking that show respect and avoid offending the other person.
old example: Using the right politeness strategies when delivering difficult news keeps the relationship intact even when the message is hard to hear.
new example: She used polite strategies to decline his request without damaging the relationship.

old definition: A communication style where meaning comes from context, tone, and relationship — not just the words. What is left unsaid often carries as much meaning as what is said.
new definition: Describing a style where meaning depends on context and relationships, not just words.
old example: In a high-context conversation, what goes unsaid is often just as important as what is said — you need to listen for the gaps.
new example: Our Japanese partners are high-context, so I listened carefully for what they left unsaid.

old definition: A communication style where meaning is stated clearly and directly. Everything important is said out loud — not implied or left to the listener to work out.
new definition: Describing a style where meaning is stated clearly and explicitly in the words.
old example: A low-context approach means putting every commitment on the table explicitly — dates, prices, deliverables, and responsibilities — so there is nothing left to interpretation.
new example: In a low-context deal, we put the price, delivery date, and support terms in writing.

old definition: A person's social reputation and dignity in a group. Helping someone save face means avoiding public embarrassment. In many cultures, this shapes how disagreement and bad news are communicated.
new definition: A person's public image and dignity in the eyes of others.
old example: Raising a concern in private rather than in front of colleagues is one of the simplest ways to help someone save face and keep the relationship strong.
new example: He raised the issue privately so the manager would not lose face.

old definition: The level of formality in your language. Register ranges from very formal (a board presentation) to casual (a team message). Choosing the right register shows you understand the relationship and the situation.
new definition: The level of formality you choose in speech or writing for a situation.
old example: Knowing when to shift register — from formal presentation language to a more conversational tone — shows you understand the relationship, not just the subject.
new example: I switched to a more casual register once the meeting ended.

old definition: Telling the other person clearly what to expect before problems happen. In cross-cultural sales, timelines, commitments, and next steps can mean different things to different people — so stating them explicitly prevents misunderstanding.
new definition: The process of making sure others know realistically what to expect from you.
old example: Clear expectation management at the start of a project — covering timelines, milestones, and what happens when things change — prevents most of the conflicts that develop later.
new example: Good expectation management meant she showed the client every milestone and risk upfront.

word: I WANT TO MAKE SURE I'M APPROACHING THIS IN A WAY THAT WORKS FOR YOU
old definition: A phrase used to show cultural awareness and invite the buyer to shape the style of the conversation. It gives them control over how you communicate, not what you say.
new definition: A polite phrase that asks the other person how they prefer to work together.
old example: I want to make sure I'm approaching this in a way that works for you — would you prefer to start with a broad overview, or go straight into the detail?
new example: I want to make sure I'm approaching this in a way that works for you.

word: I MAY BE MORE DIRECT THAN YOU'RE USED TO — PLEASE LET ME KNOW IF YOU'D PREFER A DIFFERENT APPROACH
old definition: A phrase used to name your own communication style before it causes confusion. It opens the door for the other person to ask for a different approach if needed.
new definition: A polite phrase that warns the other person about your style and invites feedback.
old example: I may be more direct than you're used to — please let me know if you'd prefer a different approach and I'll adjust.
new example: I may be more direct than you're used to, so please let me know if you'd prefer a different approach.

word: I WANT TO MAKE SURE WE'RE ALIGNED ON EXPECTATIONS BEFORE WE MOVE FORWARD
old definition: A phrase used to check that both sides agree on what happens next before anything starts. It prevents misunderstanding by making timelines, roles, and commitments explicit from the beginning.
new definition: A phrase that checks both sides agree on what to expect before starting.
old example: I want to make sure we're aligned on expectations before we move forward — particularly around the timeline and who is responsible for each stage.
new example: I want to make sure we're aligned on expectations before we move forward with the shipment.

word: IN MY EXPERIENCE WORKING WITH ORGANISATIONS IN [CONTEXT], I'VE FOUND THAT...
old definition: A phrase used to share an observation from your own experience without assuming it applies to the other person. It opens a conversation rather than making a claim.
new definition: A phrase that shares what you have learned from past work in a particular setting.
old example: In my experience working with organisations in fast-moving markets, the integration phase almost always takes longer than the initial estimate — it's worth building that into the plan now.
new example: In my experience working with organisations in the Gulf, I've found that decisions take time.

word: WHAT I HEARD YOU SAY WAS X — DID I UNDERSTAND THAT CORRECTLY?
old definition: A phrase used to confirm you understood what the buyer said, especially after an indirect or ambiguous response. Reflecting back what you heard and checking it shows care and prevents misreading.
new definition: A phrase that checks you have understood the other person correctly.
old example: What I heard you say was that budget isn't the main concern right now — it's the internal approval process. Did I understand that correctly?
new example: What I heard you say was that delivery matters most. Did I understand that correctly?

word: I NOTICE WE MAY HAVE DIFFERENT VIEWS ON THE TIMELINE — COULD YOU HELP ME UNDERSTAND YOUR THINKING?
old definition: A phrase used to raise a difference in expectations without making it feel like a conflict. It invites the other person to explain their thinking rather than defend a position.
new definition: A polite phrase that raises a disagreement and asks the other person to explain.
old example: I notice we may have different views on the timeline — could you help me understand your thinking so we can find an approach that works for both sides?
new example: I notice we may have different views on the timeline. Could you help me understand your thinking?

old definition: The extra quality and benefits that make a product worth its higher price.
new definition: The extra quality and benefits that make a product worth its higher price.
old example: Premium value is never visible in a price comparison — it lives in the quality, the support, and the structural advantages that only show up over time.
new example: The premium value of this car goes well beyond the price.

old definition: The total cost of owning something over time, including all extra costs beyond the starting price.
new definition: The full cost of owning something over time, not just the starting price.
old example: When you compare the total cost of ownership across both proposals — setup, integration, support, and renewal — the gap between the headline prices almost always narrows significantly.
new example: Over five years, the total cost of ownership clearly favours this system.

old definition: The money or value you get back from an investment over many years.
new definition: The money or value you get back from an investment over many years.
old example: The long-term return on a premium investment rarely shows its full strength in year one — it's the compounding effect across years two and three that makes the case decisive.
new example: The long-term return on this development grows stronger every single year.

old definition: The belief a customer has that you will do what you say you will do.
new definition: The belief a customer has that you will do what you say you will do.
old example: Trust at this level is built step by step — through performance data, open communication, contractual accountability, and finally a partnership that both sides have earned.
new example: Trust is why we are comfortable signing this agreement today.

old definition: When a benefit grows bigger over time because each improvement builds on the last.
new definition: When a benefit grows bigger over time because each improvement builds on the last.
old example: The compounding argument is most powerful when you show the buyer what the platform knows about their business by year three — and what leaving at that point would actually cost them.
new example: The compounding effect becomes truly dramatic from year seven onwards.

old definition: The reasons and evidence you give to show that a high price is the right choice.
new definition: The reasons and evidence showing that a high price is the right choice.
old example: A strong justification gives the buyer everything they need to defend the decision internally — verified criteria, specific comparisons, and a financial model that stands up to scrutiny.
new example: The justification for this aircraft is clear in these figures.

old definition: Actions you take to reduce the chance that something will go wrong with a purchase or investment.
new definition: Actions taken to reduce the chance that a purchase or investment goes wrong.
old example: Every major risk a buyer raises should have a specific contractual or structural response — not a reassurance, but a named protection built into the commercial terms.
new example: Our risk mitigation plan blocks every threat on this list.

old definition: A very high level of personal service where every detail is taken care of for you.
new definition: A very high level of personal service where every detail is handled.
old example: White-glove implementation means every stage is managed proactively — the client never has to chase for an update or solve a problem that should have been anticipated.
new example: Our white-glove service covers your car, your flight and your hotel.

word: THE PRICE REFLECTS THE TOTAL COST OF OWNERSHIP, NOT JUST THE LICENCE FEE
old definition: Use this to explain that the price includes all costs over time — not just the basic fee.
new definition: Use this to say the price includes every cost over time.
old example: Once you include onboarding, integration, and support in the calculation, the price reflects the total cost of ownership — and the gap between the two proposals narrows significantly.
new example: The price reflects the total cost of ownership, not just the licence fee.

word: WHAT WE'RE OFFERING IS NOT A PRODUCT — IT IS A LONG-TERM PARTNERSHIP
old definition: Use this to show the customer that you are offering a lasting relationship, not just a one-time sale.
new definition: Use this to say you offer a lasting relationship, not one sale.
old example: What we're offering is not a product with a delivery date — it is a long-term partnership whose value compounds with every quarter you use it.
new example: What we're offering is not a product, it is a long-term partnership.

word: THE QUESTION ISN'T WHETHER THIS IS EXPENSIVE — IT'S WHETHER THE RETURN JUSTIFIES THE INVESTMENT
old definition: Use this when a customer says the price is too high — it moves the conversation from cost to value.
new definition: Use this when a customer says the price is high, to focus on value.
old example: The question isn't whether this is expensive — it's whether the return justifies the investment. When you put both sides on the table, the answer becomes clear.
new example: The question isn't whether this is expensive, it's whether the return justifies the investment.

word: LET ME SHOW YOU WHAT THE COMPOUNDING RETURN LOOKS LIKE OVER THREE YEARS
old definition: Use this to show the customer how the value of your product grows bigger each year.
new definition: Use this to show how the value of your product grows each year.
old example: Let me show you what the compounding return looks like over three years — because the picture at year three is a very different conversation from the one you're having today.
new example: Let me show you what the compounding return looks like over three years.

word: TRUST AT THIS LEVEL IS EARNED, NOT CLAIMED
old definition: Use this to tell a customer you will prove you can be trusted — with evidence, not just words.
new definition: Use this to tell a customer you will prove your reliability with evidence.
old example: Trust at this level is earned — one verified layer at a time. Track record, references, and contractual accountability are the currency, not claims.
new example: Trust at this level is earned, not claimed.

word: OUR CLIENTS DON'T COME TO US BECAUSE WE'RE THE CHEAPEST OPTION — THEY COME BECAUSE THEY'VE CALCULATED WE'RE THE MOST VALUABLE
old definition: Use this to explain that your best customers chose you after comparing all options — not because you were the cheapest.
new definition: Use this to say customers chose you after comparing options, not because of low price.
old example: Our clients don't come to us because we're the cheapest option — they come because, at the end of a rigorous analysis, the premium choice is the one that makes financial sense.
new example: Our clients don't come because we're cheapest, they come because we're most valuable.

old definition: The team in a company that manages buying from outside suppliers. They check vendors, review proposals, and approve contracts before any purchase is made.
new definition: The department that handles a company's purchases from outside suppliers.
old example: Every new supplier must pass through procurement before a contract can be signed — they check policy, price, and compliance at each stage of the process.
new example: Procurement will review every vendor against our policy and budget checks.

old definition: A formal document you send to a potential client that explains your solution, pricing, and plan. It shows how your offer meets their needs.
new definition: A formal document that presents your solution, price, and plan to a potential client.
old example: The proposal was delivered in person, with each section walked through to show exactly how the solution addressed the client's stated requirements.
new example: Here is our proposal, and each section matches your priorities.

old definition: A legal document that both sides sign to confirm the deal. It sets out the price, scope, SLA, and conditions for the partnership.
new definition: A legally binding written agreement that both sides sign to confirm a deal.
old example: Both legal teams reviewed every section of the contract before either side signed — covering scope, price, timelines, and penalty terms.
new example: Both teams have reviewed the contract, and we are ready to sign.

old definition: Anyone in a company who has an interest in or influence over a buying decision. This can include finance, IT, legal, and the business team.
new definition: A person with an interest in, or influence over, a business decision.
old example: Before the deal could move forward, all the key stakeholders were mapped — from finance and legal to IT and the business sponsor — to make sure everyone was aligned.
new example: Each stakeholder on the list represents a different department in the decision.

old definition: Request for Proposal. A formal document a company sends to suppliers asking them to submit a detailed proposal. It sets out the requirements, evaluation criteria, and submission deadline.
